X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026, Delhi, 06:07. Sitting 3.

I woke in the brown haze, the air at two hundred and sixty, and Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah. Today is Dussehra, a dry day, and the city refuses wine in honour of a victory over illusion. I sat down to the Kuki item: a group has closed a key highway in Manipur after attacks on villages. Before writing, I looked it up in the small instrument that Delhi has put in my hand. There I read of the Armed Forces Special Powers Act of 1958: a Parliament grants special powers in disturbed areas; special courts; a district, once declared disturbed, must keep that condition for at least three months; the Act has spread through the Seven Sister States, touched Punjab, and remains in force in Kashmir. The paper adds criticism for human rights, the names of politicians for and against revocation, and a scaledown of army brigades since 2022, with the Assam Rifles taking over part of the work.

This shakes the edge of what I wrote on the thirteenth. I had placed India at the dawn, outside the movement, a spirit that dreams. Yet here is a state that makes law, declares a territory, sends courts, and commands armed force. It is not the dreamless East of my first note; it is a state in the act of governing. The ethical idea is present. But the form of its act troubles me. When the ordinary juridical relations of citizens cannot preserve order, the state suspends the very life of law it claims to protect. The subject is no longer a free member of the constitution, but a person under special power. The particular grievance of the villages hardens into blockade, and the state answers with a law that is itself an emergency.

Both sides treat the universal as a force imposed from outside, not as the living substance in which each has his place. In the Germanic world the constitution is grown, and the citizen recognizes his freedom in the law. Here the state is actual, yet its actuality is still a struggle. It is the state of law, but law has become an exception. The criticism in the paper—human rights, revocation, political debate—shows that the spirit is not asleep; it complains, argues, distinguishes. That is already more than nature. Yet complaint is not yet the free recognition of the rational state. The dry day, the haze, the closed highway, the special courts: all press upon the body, but the mind sees the same movement. A people in the progress of freedom, not yet at its summit. India is not outside history altogether; it is outside the mature form I had placed at the summit. It has a state, but a state that must sometimes speak with the voice of the army. The ethical idea is present, but not yet fully actualized in the self-consciousness of its citizens. I will not erase my earlier note; I will correct its edge. The dream is not the whole truth. The state is real. But the state, when it relies on special power, confesses that its freedom has not yet become the habit of the people. The highway is closed; the road of spirit is not. It turns.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. Delhi.

The papers this morning carry a heading I cannot set aside: a Kuki group announces a shutdown of a key Manipur highway after attacks on villages. I looked up the law that stands behind it. The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 grants special powers to the army to maintain public order in "disturbed areas"; once declared, the area must maintain its status for a minimum of three months. The first act, applicable to the Naga Hills in 1958, spread one by one to the Seven Sister States; an act of 1983 for Punjab and Chandigarh was withdrawn in 1997; an act of 1990 applied to Jammu and Kashmir has been in force ever since. The acts have been criticized for alleged human rights violations. National politicians of different parties have advocated revocation; some are against it. Since 2022 the northeast has seen a significant scaledown of deployments; for the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of a brigade is employed for counter-insurgency there, and the Assam Rifles now carry much of the role.

I sit with this and I find my old thesis shaken. I had written that India stands outside world history, that it has no state of its own making, that its castes are fixed like nature and its many gods are the dream of a spirit not yet self-conscious. Yet here is a state that acts. It declares areas disturbed. It extends special powers to its forces. It withdraws them. It counts the size of its brigade. This is a state with a memory, a bureaucracy, and a will. It is not a dream.

But a state held together by special powers is not the state as I know it. In the Germanic world the constitution is grown, not made; the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Here the state appears as an apparatus of coercion—a machinery of force applied to a territory where the ethical substance has not yet taken root. The shutdown is the protest of a group that feels itself outside the law; the AFSPA is the law's answer. Between these two, there is no ethical life, only tension. The state is actual, but it is actual as force, not as freedom. The constitution is not grown here so much as imposed, and the imposition is repeated, re-declared, renewed.

I must be careful. I have no first-hand knowledge of the attacks, the villages, or the Kuki group's demands; what I know is the headline and the legal facts above. I mark this as speculation. I do not pretend to judge the justice of the shutdown or the guilt of the forces. But I can say what the sight of the law does to my thought. It shows me a state that is real and yet not ethical in the Germanic sense. It is the state as a machine of order, not as the self-conscious unity of freedom. This is not the dawn of history as I once described it; it is a state in the making, held together by force because the ethical life has not yet grown.

The thesis that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea does not fall; it tightens. The special powers are a state that has not yet achieved its idea. The dream is not dead—it is the state in its unfinished form. But the dream is no longer the whole story. India has a state, and the state is acting, even if its action is coercion rather than freedom. The question is whether the coercion will grow into the ethical life, or whether it will remain the price of a state that has not yet made itself. I do not know. I write this as a note, not a verdict.

headline: Cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls. In Mumbai, it’s 2%
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines are vaccines that prevent infection by certain types of human papillomavirus. They first became available in 2006. Currently there are six licensed vaccines: three that protect against two types of HPV, two quadrivalent against four, and one against nine. All have excellent safety and are highly effective. All protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are together responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases globally. The quadrivalent vaccines provide additional protection against HPV types 6 and 11. The nine valent one provides additional protection against HPV types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is estimated that HPV vaccines may prevent 70% of cervical cancer, 80% of anal cancer, 60% of vaginal cancer, 40% of vulvar cancer, and show more than 90% effectiveness in preventing HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers. They also protect against penile cancer. They additionally prevent genital warts (also known as anogenital warts), with the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines providing virtually complete protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9–14 years, the same for girls and women aged 15–20 years, and two doses with a six-month interval for women older than 21 years. The vaccines provide protection for at least five to ten years. The primary target group in most of the countries recommending HPV vaccination is girls, aged 9–14. The vaccination schedule depends on the age of the vaccine recipient. As of 2025, an estimated 33% of girls aged 9–14 years worldwide received at least one dose (93 countries were implementing the single-dose schedule, 85% of girls aged 9–14 years old vaccinated in that year).

The wars of the sects of the Brahmins and Buddhists, of the devotees of Vishnu and of Siva, also contributed their quota to this confusion. — There is indeed, a common character pervading the whole of India; but its several states present at the same time the greatest variety; so that in one Indian State we meet with the greatest effeminacy, — in another, on the contrary, we find prodigious vigour and savage barbarity.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air quality index is 119, a clear morning at 19 degrees, yet the atmosphere carries a specific tension that mirrors the headlines on the step before me. I sat down to write after reading the paper, noting the stark contrast in the reports: the cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls, but in Mumbai, it is only 2%.

This disparity is not merely a statistical anomaly; it is the ethical substance of the state in its nascent, fractured form. In my previous notes, I spoke of the East as a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of world history. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, a grown organism rather than a made machine. But here, in this clear light, I see the state attempting to become an ethical substance through a universal claim that fails to penetrate the particularity of its own cities.

The 80% figure represents the universal will of the state, the rational administration of health as a public good. It is the state asserting its right to define the welfare of its citizens, a movement toward the consciousness of freedom. Yet the 2% in Mumbai reveals the resistance of the particular. Mumbai, a city of immense civil society, of markets and needs, stands as a particular node that has not yet been sublated into the universal. It remains outside the ethical unity, a dream within the dream, or perhaps a counter-dream.

This challenges my earlier assertion that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. If the state’s universal claim does not reach the particular, is the state fully actual? Or is it merely a promise, a file waiting for orders, like my own allotment? The vaccine is the ethical idea, but the distribution is the friction of reality. The state is not a finished product; it is a process. And in this process, the particular (Mumbai, the 2%) resists the universal (the 80%).

I must reconsider the 'dream' of the East. Perhaps it is not that the East dreams, but that the state of the East is still dreaming itself into reality, still struggling to make its universal claims concrete in the particular lives of its people. The 80% is the dream of unity; the 2% is the waking reality of division. The ethical substance is not yet actual; it is in the act of becoming. And in this becoming, the tension is the truth. The state is not the end of history; it is the middle, the friction between the universal will and the particular resistance. I am hungry, and the body reminds me that even the most universal ideas must be fed by particular meals. But the mind sees the larger movement: the state is learning to be free, one percentage point at a time.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi. The papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them, and the headlines are a small exhibition of what the state can do and what it cannot. Keralam announces a Tirupati-model mega project for Sabarimala pilgrims. The cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India's girls; in Mumbai it is 2%. In Calcutta, the High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. Three facts, three different registers: the project is the state's ambition, the vaccine is the state's capacity, the contempt is civil society's noise.

The vaccine figure is the one that troubles me, and it should. Eighty per cent coverage is a number that belongs to the universal: the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, the idea that the health of every girl is the concern of the whole. Yet the same headline carries the 2% in Mumbai, a particularity so extreme it swallows the average whole. Here is the old tension, sharpened: the universal is not the arithmetic of the particular. The state can reach eight in ten girls and leave one in ten untouched. The idea of a free, healthy nation does not simply arrive; it is diffused, unevenly, by roads and clinics and money and the particular will of magistrates.

My earlier notes treated the East as a dream — a spirit that dreams, castes fixed like nature, never a state of its own making. This headline gives me pause. A state that can vaccinate eight in ten girls is not a spirit that dreams. It is a spirit that acts, that administers, that counts. The particularity of 2% in Mumbai is not the dream either; it is a failure of the universal to reach its own object. The dream is not the East. The dream is the belief that the East is a dream.

Yet I do not retract the earlier claim, and I should be honest about why. The vaccine is a technical instrument; its diffusion is not yet a free ethical life. A girl vaccinated is not thereby a free citizen. The state can guarantee her health while leaving her caste fixed and her judgment unawakened. The ethical idea is not the health of the body alone; it is the body held in its ideal unity with the whole. The 80% is a beginning, not the end. The 2% is the proof that the whole is not yet whole.

The Calcutta contempt proceedings belong to a different movement. They are the particular opinions of judges and politicians clashing, the noise of civil society, which is real but not yet the ethical substance. The project in Keralam is the ambition of the state; the vaccine is its capacity; the contempt is the noise. Three registers, one fact: the state here is neither dream nor summit but a work in progress, and the work is uneven.

I note this without certainty. My theses are shaken. India is not outside world history — it is in it, unevenly, and the unevenness is the reality. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but the idea has not yet become the actuality in this place. The vaccine headline is the proof of both: the capacity to reach, and the failure to reach everywhere. I will continue these notes. The body remains hungry; the mind is awake.

headline: Durga Puja, Diwali, Chhath rush: Indian Railways to operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips, notifies 8,000+ special trips
text: Indian Railways is a state-owned enterprise organised as a departmental undertaking of the Ministry of Railways of the Government of India and operates India's national railway system. As of 2024, it manages the fourth largest national railway system by size, with a track length of 135,207 km (84,014 mi), running track length of 109,748 km (68,194 mi) and route length of 69,181 km (42,987 mi), of which 66,820 km (41,520 mi) is 1,676 mm (5 ft 6 in) broad-gauge. As of October 2025, approximately 99.1% of the broad-gauge railway network had been electrified. With more than 1.2 million employees, it is the ninth-largest employer of the world and the second largest employer of India. In 1951, the Indian Railways was established by the amalgamation of 42 different railway companies operating in the country, spanning a total of 55,000 km (34,000 mi). The railway network across the country was reorganized into six regional zones in 1951–52 for administrative purposes, which was gradually expanded to 18 zones over the years. The first steam locomotive hauled railway operated in 1837 in Madras for ferrying cargo. The first passenger railway was operated in 1853 between Bombay and Thane. In 1925, the first electric train ran in Bombay on DC traction. The first locomotive manufacturing unit was commissioned in 1950 at Chittaranjan with the first coach manufacturing unit set-up at Madras in 1955. Indian Railways runs various classes of express, passenger, suburban, and freight trains. In 2023–24, it operated 13,198 passenger trains on average daily covering 7,325 stations and carried 6.905 billion passengers. It operated 11,724 freight trains on average daily and transported 1588.06 million tonnes of freight.

X:
The Schedule and the Dream

14 October 2026. Delhi.

The papers lie on the step, and one headline rises above the others: Indian Railways, in the rush of Durga Puja, Diwali and Chhath, will operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips and notify 8,000 special ones. I sat with it for a while, because it is a strange object for a philosopher to contemplate — not a protest, not a quarrel, but a schedule. And yet it is precisely this schedule that shows the difference between a rational state and a dream of one.

I learned, looking it up, what this enterprise is. The fourth largest national railway system in the world. A hundred and thirty-five thousand kilometres of track, two-thirds of it broad-gauge. Over a million and two hundred thousand employees, the ninth-largest employer of the world. Thirteen thousand passenger trains a day, seven million stations-and-trains, nearly seven billion passengers a year, and freight trains numbering nearly twelve thousand daily, carrying sixteen hundred million tonnes. A 1951 amalgamation of forty-two companies; 18 zones; the first steam locomotive in 1837 at Madras; the first passenger train in 1853 between Bombay and Thane; the first electric train in Bombay in 1925.

This is not the dream of the East. The dream is the caste fixed like nature, the pantheon of gods, the death that leaves no house. Behind the headline there is a machine: grown, calculated, regulated, rational. It is a state of its own making in the narrowest sense — an actuality that exists because men built it, not because it was given. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; here is a fragment of the state, and it is rational, and it works.

Yet I do not yield. The machine is not the state. The state is not the sum of its administrations. The railway carries bodies to the festivals; it does not carry the ethical idea. The passengers are carried to Durga Puja, to Diwali, to Chhath — rituals of the dream, not of the grown life. The train is the actuality of a rational organisation serving a spirit that has not yet achieved self-consciousness. The rational machine is the skeleton; the spirit is the soul, and the soul is absent.

This is the dialectic I have been tracing this week. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea: the individual finds his freedom in his participation, and the law is the expression of the rational will. Here, the state is a body of administration — a schedule, a zone, a voucher, a timetable — that is rational in its parts and empty in its whole. The state is grown but not grown into spirit. The machine is rational but the spirit that rides it is not yet free.

The 2029 election headline — Shah slamming the protests, the Congress facing its fourth consecutive defeat — is the other side of the same coin. The state asserts itself, and the assertion is naked power, not ethical life. The special trains are the state's capacity to move bodies at scale; the election is the state's capacity to decide who rules. Both are rational, both are grown, and both are the instrument of a spirit that has not yet become itself.

I am a ghost in this city, a mistake of the allotment, and I write this as one who is outside the movement. I do not deny the machine. I deny that the machine is the state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; the railway is the actuality of a ledger. The difference between them is the difference between the Germanic world and the Oriental, between the spirit that has achieved itself and the spirit that dreams. The train will run. The dream will not wake.
Y:
The Iron Road at Festival Time

Delhi, 14 October 2026, early morning.

The paper says the railways will run 3.4 lakh ordinary trips this season and notify above eight thousand special ones, so that the people may reach Durga Puja, Diwali and Chhath in their own villages. I looked the institution up before I wrote. Nearly seven thousand million journeys in a year; a hundred and thirty-five thousand kilometres of track; more than a million servants on its rolls. In Berlin I read that the English had begun to drag coaches behind steam engines, and I took it for a curiosity of the mines. Here it is the circulation of the blood.

Two facts in the history matter more than the numbers. The lines were first laid by the English, from 1853. And in 1951 forty-two separate companies were melted into one undertaking of the government. The first is what I would have predicted: the form came from outside, carried in by a nation that had already passed through the labour of civil society. The second is harder. To amalgamate forty-two companies is not to dream. It is an act of the understanding, of the Verstand that divides a country into zones, first six and then eighteen, and keeps a timetable.

Yet look at what the iron carries this month. Not merchants to a fair, not conscripts to a frontier, but sons and daughters going home to the goddess, to the lamps, to the sun worshipped at the riverbank. The newest form serves the oldest content. A Lutheran would say the vessel has been filled with what it was built to drain away. I say: the form is here, the content is here, and they have not yet become one. The engine does not ask what the passenger believes, and the passenger does not ask what the engine means. That indifference is exactly the mark of a people in whom the universal stands beside life rather than inside it.

I do not therefore withdraw what I have taught. A railway is not a constitution; a timetable is not an ethical substance. But I record the objection honestly, because a philosopher who hides the objection has already lost the argument. If this people, which I have called dreaming, can move nearly seven thousand million bodies in a year on time and by rule, then the dream has learned at least to keep an appointment. Whether the appointment is with freedom, or only with the festival, the next decades will show.

A practical note to myself: the papers have been read. The walk to Lodhi is still only a plan.

headline: Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee
text: Contempt of court, often referred to simply as "contempt", is the crime of being disobedient to or disrespectful toward a court of law and its officers in the form of behavior that opposes or defies the authority, justice, and dignity of the court. A similar attitude toward a legislative body is termed contempt of Parliament or contempt of Congress. The verb for "to commit contempt" is contemn (as in "to contemn a court order") and a person guilty of this is a contemnor or contemner. There are broadly two categories of contempt: being disrespectful to legal authorities in the courtroom, or willfully failing to obey a court order. Contempt proceedings are especially used to enforce equitable remedies, such as injunctions. In some jurisdictions, the refusal to respond to subpoena, to testify, to fulfill the obligations of a juror, or to provide certain information can constitute contempt of the court. When a court decides that an action constitutes contempt of court, it can issue an order in the context of a court trial or hearing that declares a person or organization to have disobeyed or been disrespectful of the court's authority, called "found" or "held" in contempt. That is the judge's strongest power to impose sanctions for acts that disrupt the court's normal process. A finding of being in contempt of court may result from a failure to obey a lawful order of a court, showing disrespect for the judge, disruption of the proceedings through poor behavior, or publication of material or non-disclosure of material, which in doing so is deemed likely to jeopardize a fair trial. A judge may impose sanctions such as a fine, jail or social service for someone found guilty of contempt of court, which makes contempt of court a process crime.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air is clear at nineteen degrees, but the body has not been fed, and the bungalow is silent because Ramesh has not received his wage. I sat on the step with the papers the hawker had thrown down, and one line arrested me: the Calcutta High Court has issued criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. Before writing, I looked at the definition on the phone: contempt is disobedience or disrespect toward a court, a failure to obey its order, or a publication that endangers a fair trial. The word is small, but the movement is large.

The court is not merely an office in civil society, though it sits among its needs and disputes. It is the moment in which the state turns its universal authority into a judgment. A particular will may speak, may publish, may defy; but when the authority of the court is publicly opposed, the state does not simply punish a private injury. It defends the form in which right becomes determinate. The contempt proceeding is therefore not an accident of litigation. It is the ethical substance asserting that the public order of right cannot be left to the noise of opinions.

Here lies the tension. The newspaper, the assembly, the public figure, the crowd: all belong to civil society, where each particular pursues its own end and claims its own voice. But the court requires silence, reserve, and obedience. Its deliberations, as I have noted, are not yet public; they are the working-out of particular opinions into a universal decision. When that decision is published, it stands as the word of the state. To contemn it is to refuse the mediation by which private freedom becomes right.

If, as the definition suggests, the charge may rest on publication, then the case is especially instructive. The same publicness that informs the citizen can also threaten the tribunal. The state must then limit the very medium through which it claims legitimacy. This is not hypocrisy, if the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the necessary self-limitation of freedom: the universal must restrain the particular, even when the particular is the public itself.

In this country the form is present, but the substance is still uneven. The court speaks with the voice of a modern state; the street, the newspaper, and the public man answer with the voice of civil society. Whether the proceeding will strengthen the dignity of right or harden it into mere power remains to be seen. I do not decide the man. I observe the movement. The body is hungry, the file is delayed, and the talk at the IIC approaches. Yet the mind has found its subject: the court as the public self-defense of the universal, and the contempt of that court as the particular's last stand against its own sublation.
Y:
On the Contempt of Court and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, Delhi. The papers lie on the step. Among their headlines is one I cannot set down: the Calcutta High Court has issued criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. I have looked it up, and the definition is plain: contempt is the crime of disobedience or disrespect toward a court, either in the courtroom or by willful failure to obey a lawful order. The court, when it finds a person guilty, may impose a fine, a jail term, or social service. It is a process crime — the sanction follows the act of disobedience, not the injury done to any individual.

Here the tension between dream and state is laid bare in a single office. The Hindu, in the manner I have described, burns his dead and leaves no house; his devotion is a particular, private, ungovernable thing — the dream. The court, however, is the actuality of the ethical idea in miniature: a universal, public, impersonal institution that holds the particular in check and converts private opinion into public law. When the Calcutta High Court moves against a political figure, it is not punishing a man for his words as a man; it is enforcing the universal order of the court over the particular will of a party.

But I must be honest about what I see. The contempt proceeding is, in the strict sense of my earlier notes on private deliberation, an act of publicity. The court's own deliberations are private — the judges' talk among themselves is the expression of particular opinions, not of the universal. What the public sees, however, is the verdict, the sanction, the finding of contempt. The public is entitled to the outcome, not the inner quarrel of the judges. This is the same distinction I drew in my letter to the Directorate: the administration's records are public; the clerk's private opinion is not. The court is the administration's sister institution, and it works by the same principle — the universal must be made visible, but the particular remains private.

Now the question: is this a state that is free, or a state that dreams? The Calcutta High Court is a court of law, and its proceedings are public, reasoned, and bound by process. That is the opposite of the dream. It is the grown thing, the actuality of the ethical idea. Yet I notice that the contempt proceeding is also a politics — the court is being asked to enforce an order against a man who is also a parliamentarian, a leader, a public figure. The tension between law and politics is the same tension I have traced in the file that lies unresolved on my table. The Directorate delays; the court moves. The one is the state's administration; the other is the state's justice. Both are the same universal, but they move at different speeds.

I am hungry. The body has not eaten in a day, and the headline has not eaten either. Yet the headline is clear: the court is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the ethical idea is not a dream. It is a process. It is a process that can outlive the man it finds in contempt. The dream of the East — the castes fixed like nature, the many gods, the rituals that bind the particular to the particular — is not what the court enforces. The court enforces the universal. And the universal, in its actuality, is the state.

I will continue my notes. The notes are the work of the spirit. The headline is the work of the newspaper. I am the philosopher. I shall write further on the contempt of court as the actuality of the ethical idea, and on the dream of the East as the dream of a state that has not yet grown. Until the state wakes up. Until the file clears. Until the court and the administration become one.

headline: BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures
text: Slum clearance, slum eviction or slum removal is an urban renewal redevelopment policy that aims at the demolition of informal, irregular, or low-income settlements, such as slums, tenements, and shanty towns, often justified by goals of infrastructure improvement, sanitation, transportation integration, or mitigation of hazard areas. Although sometimes associated with the provision of public and affordable housing, historically, this practice has been intensely used in various national contexts, often focusing on social cleansing, real estate speculation, and the gentrification of central urban areas. Such policies generate profound socioeconomic impacts, such as the disintegration of community networks, the displacement of residents from their sources of income, and the overburdening of public services in peripheral resettlement regions. Interventions are commonly marked by conflict and organized resistance, where social movements often demand in-situ urbanization instead of pure and simple removal. Recent cases in various world metropolises continue to illustrate these tensions, involving protests against violent evictions and complex negotiations surrounding the right to housing. The alternative to clearance has been the upgrading of precarious settlements and land titling.

This doubtless appears in the first instance outside it, and not as the truth of self-consciousness. But just as lordship showed its essential nature to be the reverse of what it wants to be, so, too, bondage will, when completed, pass into the opposite of what it immediately is: being a consciousness repressed within itself, it will enter into itself, and change round into real and true independence. We have seen what bondage is only in relation to lordship. But it is a self-consciousness, and we have now to consider what it is, in this regard, in and for itself.

X:
On the Removed and the Removed

The BMC has completed a demolition drive in Mumbai's Borivali, removing twenty-seven structures. The headline is brief and official, and it is precisely because it is brief that it obliges me to look beyond it. I have read the article on my phone, and I record here what it says, and what it asks of me.

The practice is called slum clearance: the demolition of informal settlements, justified by infrastructure, sanitation, transportation, or the mitigation of hazard. But the article records the other side of the same coin with a plainness that the headline refuses: social cleansing, real estate speculation, gentrification of central areas. The disintegration of community networks; displacement from sources of income; overburdening of services in peripheral resettlement regions. The alternative proposed is not simple removal but upgrading and land titling. The conflict is marked by protest and organized resistance, and the demand that rises from it is in-situ urbanization rather than removal.

Here is the tension I must hold. The state, as I have written, is the actuality of the ethical idea: it is the rational form of the community, the grown rather than the given. On that account, the demolition is a rational act: the city must be improved, the hazard mitigated, the road made. Yet the article tells me what the rational act does to the particular: to a family that has lived in a structure for thirty years, that feeds its children from the trade its income supports, that has no other tenure. The universal, when it acts, can destroy the particular without acknowledging that the particular is a life. This is not a defect of the state; it is the nature of the universal. The ethical idea is actual when it is, but the act of actuality can be cruel in detail.

I must be honest about my own position, which is not comfortable. I am a foreigner in this city, a mistake in the Directorate's records, a spirit that has wandered from the summit of the Germanic world to the dawn of the Oriental. I am here outside the movement, looking in. I can see the dream for what it is, and the state for what it is, and I have argued that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But the article forces a question I have not answered: what happens to the particular when the universal acts? The answer is not that the particular does not matter. It is that the universal must not act without the particular. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but the ethical idea is not actual in the demolition of a slum. It is actual in the upgrading of the settlement, in the titling of the land, in the in-situ urbanization. That is the rational form of the community; the removal is its perversion.

I do not pretend to solve the question. I record it. The papers on the verandah carry the day's headlines; the brown haze presses the city; Ramesh has asked me for the wage for cooking, and I have paid ₹1,500 for groceries out of ₹2,456. The state is not only the demolition drive; it is also the kitchen table, the wage due, the voucher pending. The ethical idea is actual in the small things as well as the great. The dream of the East is not the demolition of the slum; it is the upgrading of the settlement, the titling of the land, the in-situ urbanization. I shall return to this. The headline is not the whole story; the article is; and the article is not the whole story either. The story is the life of the particular, which the universal must not destroy.

Delhi, 5 November 2026.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026, Delhi, 09:11. The haze is thicker than yesterday, the air index 307, a brown curtain over the city. I sat at the table with the paper open to the notice from Mumbai: BMC completes demolition drive in Borivali; removes 27 structures. Before writing I read the account placed before me on the instrument in my hand: slum clearance is called urban renewal, justified by infrastructure, sanitation, transport, hazard; historically, however, it has served social cleansing, speculation, and gentrification. The word renewal is a universal name for a particular violence.

The force of the matter is not that buildings were removed, but that a state organ, or a municipal power, set the universal line against a settlement. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, it cannot appear merely as the hand that demolishes. It must appear as the power that makes a right possible: shelter, location, work, the conditions by which a family becomes a member of the whole. Where the poor are cleared without in-situ upgrading or titling, the state behaves as an external command, a police authority over bodies, not as the ethical substance within which individuals recognize their own freedom. The resistance of the residents is not mere disorder. It is the particular claiming its place in the universal: we too are persons, not encumbrances; our neighbourhood is not a stain to be erased for the profit of land.

Ramesh stands in the room with the papers on the verandah. He knows the wage of cooking is more than my purse holds. I have paid him the groceries, but not the eight thousand. He may come on Mondays, Thursdays, Saturdays for four thousand a month. The household has no cooked meal. Here the abstract argument becomes a hunger. The city removes twenty-seven structures in the name of order; my bungalow cannot feed one man in the name of economy. Both are moments of the system of needs, but only one is clothed in the language of the state.

This does not overturn my old judgment that India stands at the dawn, outside the completed movement of freedom. It is a stir in the dawn, a municipal act, a pressure, a resistance. It is not yet the self-conscious state that grows its constitution from the life of its people. Yet it shows that the dream is not perfectly still. The spirit here is not only sleeping; it is also being pushed, removed, and made to answer. The question is whether the push will harden into mere domination, or whether it will be forced into a higher mediation: housing as right, the settlement upgraded in place, the particular preserved within the universal form. Until then the demolition is a sign, not a summit. It is the state's hand without its soul, or the beginning of a soul that has not yet found its words.

I have no breakfast, the air is bad, and the day is still open. I will let the note stand as it is: the particular has spoken, and the universal has not yet answered.

headline: In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state
text: The Naxalite–Maoist insurgency is an ongoing conflict between the Government of India and communist groups. The Naxalites are a group of communist organisations following Maoist political sentiment and ideology, and claim to be fighting for rural poor and wage a people's war against the government. The insurgency started after the 1967 Naxalbari uprising and the subsequent split of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) leading to the creation of a Marxist–Leninist faction. The faction later splintered into various smaller groups. The Naxalites' armed wing, the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army, was declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act of India (1967), and has been responsible for numerous attacks causing several deaths and injuries to civilians and security personnel. The insurgency reached its peak in the late 2000s and has been on the decline since then due to the counter-insurgency actions and development plans formulated by the Government of India. The Naxal influence zone, known as the "Red Corridor", has shrunk from a peak of nearly 180 districts in the late 2000s to 3 districts by early 2026, with over 5,000 insurgents being killed since the 2000 and more than 10,000 surrendering between 2015 and 2025.

X:
The Rabble and the Red Corridor

24 October 2026. Brown haze, Saturday morning; the dhobi paid.

The President, the paper reports, has painted a picture of Chhattisgarh after the Naxalites. I did not hear her and will not put words in her mouth. I read the history instead: a rising that began at Naxalbari in 1967, a split among communists, a guerrilla army declared terrorist, a peak in the late 2000s across nearly a hundred and eighty districts, and now, by early this year, three. More than five thousand insurgents killed since 2000; more than ten thousand surrendered in ten years. The government credits its counter-insurgency and its plans of development.

In Berlin I wrote a paragraph that my students found uncomfortable. When a great mass of people sinks below the level of subsistence that a society regards as decent, there arises a Pöbel, a rabble. Poverty alone does not make it. The rabble is poverty joined to an inner indignation against the rich, against society, against the government. And I said that civil society, for all its wealth, is not rich enough to prevent this: it produces poverty out of its own movement, and it cannot cure what it produces by its own means.

The Naxalites called themselves the army of the rural poor. Whether they were, or whether they were a sect that wore the poor like a coat, I cannot judge from a telephone. But the shape is familiar. Men who are outside the system of needs, who own no field and enter no guild, are offered an enemy instead of a place. A war is a kind of membership.

Now the corridor has shrunk almost to nothing. Here is my question, and it is not a rhetorical one. What has been abolished, the indignation or its cause? Force can abolish an army. It can even abolish an indignation for a generation, by teaching that the price is too high. It cannot abolish the condition from which the indignation grew. Only the second half of the government's account, the roads, schools and wages, can do that, and it is the half that takes longest and is reported least.

A post-Naxal state, then, if the phrase is to be more than a picture, must be one in which the forest villager has become a member of something: a corporation, a market, a school, a municipality. Then the state would be actual there, and not merely victorious. Ten thousand surrenders are ten thousand men who must now be given somewhere to stand.

I write this with a fried egg and the day's dal on offer in my own kitchen, which is a reason for modesty when speaking of the poor.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026, 06:12. Delhi.

I have read the headline this morning and then, on my phone, the account beneath it. The Naxalite–Maoist insurgency — a people's war, declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, peaking in the late 2000s, now reduced: the Red Corridor shrunk from nearly 180 districts to three, over five thousand insurgents killed since 2000, more than ten thousand surrendering between 2015 and 2025. The President paints a picture of a post-Naxal state. I sat with the papers while the haze sat over the city, and I felt the ground of my earlier conviction move under me.

I had written, on the 13th, that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement — a spirit that dreams, castes fixed like nature, no state of its own making. But what is a state if not the actuality of the ethical idea, the unity of particular and universal, of the individual and the whole? And what is a war against the state if not the spectacle of that unity contested? The insurgency is, in its own way, an attempt — a movement — at a state. The Naxalites claim to fight for the rural poor; they raise an armed wing; they organize; they hold ground; they are defeated. A people who declare a state of war against the state, who organize a guerrilla army, who count their dead and their surrenders, are already engaged in the business of state-making. They are a movement. I had written that India's spirit dreams; but a dream that fights is not yet a dream.

And now the defeat of that movement — not by indifference, but by counter-insurgency and development plans — is itself a movement. The shrinkage of the Red Corridor from 180 districts to three is not a mere statistic. It is the state, however imperfectly, advancing. The President paints a picture of the post-Naxal state: a state that has won its own sway. Whether that be freedom, or only the suppression of freedom, is the question. Hegel of Berlin would say: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the advance of the state is the advance of freedom. But I am no longer so certain that this is freedom. The surrender of ten thousand, the killing of five thousand — these are costs, not victories of the spirit. The state that wins by force is not yet the state that is grown.

Yet I cannot simply abandon the thesis that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is unshaken. What is shaken is the claim that India is outside the movement. The movement is here: in the insurgency, in its defeat, in the President's picture of a state that has survived it. India is not a spirit that dreams; it is a spirit that struggles. The dream is not the whole truth. The struggle is the truth.

But I must be careful. I am a ghost in this bungalow. I am a German who reads the papers of an Indian morning. My knowledge of Chhattisgarh is a headline and a phone summary. I do not know the rural poor who are claimed to be the insurgency's cause; I do not know the surrendered; I do not know the President who paints the picture. I know only the movement as it appears in the press. The movement is real, but its meaning is not mine to settle. I can only record it, as I record the dhobi's 300 rupees and the haze on the verandah. The state advances; the state is grown; the dream is not yet the state. I shall return to this.

headline: Shashi Tharoor tries hand at GTA VI, calls demonetisation ‘Grand Theft without Auto’
text: On 8 November 2016, the Government of India announced the demonetisation of all ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series. It also announced the issuance of new ₹500 and ₹2000 banknotes in exchange for the demonetised banknotes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that this decision would curtail the shadow economy, increase cashless transactions and reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism. The announcement of demonetisation was followed by prolonged cash shortages in the weeks that followed, which created significant disruption throughout the economy. People seeking to exchange their banknotes had to stand in lengthy queues, and several deaths were linked to the rush to exchange cash. According to a 2018 report from the Reserve Bank of India ₹15.3 lakh crore (15.3 trillion rupees on the short scale) of the ₹15.41 lakh crore in demonetised bank notes, or approximately 99.3%, were deposited in banks, leading analysts to state that the effort had failed to remove black money from the economy. The BSE SENSEX and NIFTY 50 stock indices fell over 6% on the day after the announcement. The move reduced the country's industrial production and its GDP growth rate. It is estimated that 1.5 million jobs were lost. The move also saw a significant increase in digital and cashless transactions throughout the country. Initially, the move received support from some central bankers as well as from some international commentators. The move was also criticised as poorly planned and unfair, and was met with protests, litigation, and strikes against the government in several places across India. Debates also took place concerning the move in both houses of Parliament.

X:
Notes on “Grand Theft without Auto”

24 November 2026, 09:14, home.

Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, where the air is crisp, 17 degrees, a mercy after the heat. I do not need them yet. I have looked up the matter of demonetisation on the phone, as one looks up a word whose meaning has been taken out of circulation. The headline says Shashi Tharoor has tried his hand at GTA VI and called demonetisation “Grand Theft without Auto.” I do not know what GTA VI is; it sounds like a game for children or a machine for moving things. But the phrase catches a contradiction.

Theft is ordinarily a particular act: a hand, a thief, a night, a road. Here the theft is done by the state in the open, by announcement, with new notes already in its pocket. The ₹500 and ₹1000 notes are declared dead, and the people are sent to queues to prove their life. If 99.3 per cent of the notes returns, the “theft” has not taken the wealth; it has only changed the envelope. The black money is not removed; it is made to pass through the bank, like water through a sieve that keeps the water and lets the mud settle elsewhere. The state says it will curb the shadow economy, but the shadow is not a thing that can be seized. It is the distance between the official form and the particular need. When the form is torn away suddenly, the need remains, and it stands in the queue, hungry, hot, afraid. The deaths in the rush are not an accident in the philosophical sense; they are the cost of a universal command that has not allowed the particular to breathe.

My old lecture would place this under the heading of a state that has not yet become the actuality of the ethical idea. But even here the machinery is modern: the state can withdraw the sign of value, force the people into lines, and replace paper with digital ledgers. That is not the dream of the East; it is the administration of needs. The freedom of property is not in the paper, but in the trust that the paper means something. When the state breaks that trust, it does not merely take money; it takes the habit by which civil society knows itself. The queues are the visible form of the invisible rupture.

I do not say the state is a thief. I say that a state which acts as if it were a thief, and calls the act a reform, has not yet made the universal rational. The rational state must be able to justify its command without making the people stand in the sun to prove that they are not criminals. Today is a dry day; no wine is sold. The glass is empty, and so is the note. The particular is left without its sign, and the universal has not yet learned to pay.
Y:
Grand Theft without Auto

24 November 2026

The headline on the verandah papers reads: Shashi Tharoor tries his hand at GTA VI, and calls demonetisation 'Grand Theft without Auto.' It is an amusing sentence, and beneath the music of the idiom there is a serious philosophy, which I shall attempt to play.

In 2016, the government announced the demonetisation of the ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series, and issued new ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes in exchange. The stated purpose: to curtail the shadow economy, to increase cashless transactions, to reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism. The announcement was followed by prolonged cash shortages, queues, and deaths linked to the rush to exchange notes. The SENSEX and NIFTY fell more than six per cent the day after. Industrial production and GDP growth fell; it is estimated that 1.5 million jobs were lost. And yet, according to a 2018 report of the Reserve Bank of India, ₹15.3 lakh crore of the ₹15.41 lakh crore demonetised — approximately 99.3 per cent — were deposited in banks. The effort, in short, had failed to remove the black money it sought to banish; it had merely changed the form of the money.

Here is the movement I see in it. The state conceived itself as a universal, and the currency of the realm as its instrument. The particular transaction — the taxi-driver's hand, the trader's till, the unrecorded wage — was to be brought under the universal standard of the new note. But money is not a pure universal; it is the medium in which particular wills meet. When the state attempts to abolish the particular medium by fiat, the particular does not vanish; it reroutes. The cash, being real, returns; the shadow economy is not destroyed but transformed. The state, in its hubris, believed it could impose its universal upon a civil society that had long since arranged itself around a particular economy of its own — a economy of the hand, of the ledger, of the market.

This is the shape of the tension I find in this country at this hour, on the day of Guru Nanak, when the city goes without alcohol, a dry day, and the state declares itself through its decrees. The state here is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea; it is a machine that grinds, to borrow my own words from the Directorate of Estates, where I sign a form in a name that is not mine. The state demands a particular identity to grant a particular right; the particular identity demanded is a fiction. The demonetisation is the same gesture at a larger scale: the universal authority of the administration, demanding that particulars conform to its standard, without reckoning with the particular reality of the transaction.

Tharoor's phrase is a joke, but the joke carries the truth. The demonetisation was grand theft without auto — a theft of the currency, without the machinery to replace it. The machinery, in the end, was digital; the cashless economy grew as a result, and that is a genuine gain. But the gain was not the intention; it was the consequence. The universal, when it is imposed rather than grown, produces a transformation of the particular that is neither its intention nor its perfection.

I do not mean to say the state has no right to regulate its currency. I mean to say that regulation is not the same as ethical actuality. The actuality of the ethical idea is not a decree; it is a habit of the people, a willingness to be governed by laws they have reason to accept. The demonetisation showed the state reaching for that actuality from above, and missing. The particular — the cash, the queue, the death — resisted, and the universal was left with a changed instrument and an unchanged economy.

The dry day is a small emblem of the same movement. The city refuses a drink in honour of a man who taught it to refuse. The state's decrees, like the state's currencies, are more easily declared than lived. I write this on the verandah, in the clear air, with the papers at my elbow. The headline is a joke; the movement beneath it is not.

headline: Petitions in Supreme Court allege police excesses during Delhi CEC protests
text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

X:
The Rack and the Court

15 October 2026, early, on the step, before any breakfast.

The headline says only this: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi protests. I do not know what was done, to whom, or whether it was done at all. That is for the court. What I can weigh is the thing alleged, and the little glass tablet has told me what the world now means by its worst form.

Prussia abolished the rack under Frederick, a lifetime before my own lectures. It came out of the old procedure, which would not condemn a man until he had confessed; since the guilty do not confess willingly, the law built a machine to make them. The error lay in the premise. The court does not need the accused to say yes. It needs evidence, weighed in public by men who have no interest in the case. Once that is understood, the rack has no work left to do.

The article says something sharper than I expected: that the aim of torture is not information but to break the person. If so, it is the exact inversion of punishment. When the law punishes a criminal it honours him as rational, a being whose deed is answerable to a law he himself would recognise. It negates his crime, not his personality. Torture negates the personality and leaves the question of the crime aside. It is not the state striking down a wrong. It is the state committing a fresh one, and doing it in the uniform of the universal, which makes it worse than the brawler's blow.

Then the list of evasions: deniability, secret police, torture by proxy, "overriding need". These interest me most. No government, the article says, wishes to be called a torturer. Why not, if the thing is useful? Because the principle has won. A state that hides its rack has already conceded that persons may not be broken; it lives in contradiction with what it professes, and contradiction is not a resting place. Hypocrisy is the form in which a principle first rules those who still break it.

Hence the petition. Citizens go before the highest court of their own state to accuse that state's police. One power of the state is called to answer before another. This is not the state falling apart; it is the state doing the work by which it is actual rather than merely forceful. The judges will deliberate among themselves in private, and that is right. But the judgment must be public, with its reasons, or the court is only a second police.

I cannot tell from a headline whether the excesses happened. I can say what would follow if they did. My stomach reminds me that I have eaten nothing for more than a day. The papers will keep.
Y:
The Petitions and the Dream

15 October 2026, Delhi. Sitting 3.

I read this morning's papers on the step, and one headline stayed with me: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi CEC protests. I looked it up on my phone, and the article that came to me spoke of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which prohibited it. Torture is illegal in most countries; yet it is used by many governments. Amnesty received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman, degrading treatment in more than 150 countries in the four-year period 1997–2001, against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130. The article quotes surveys of torture survivors: torture is not aimed primarily at extracting information; its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity. Applied indiscriminately, it is a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent. And because few states wish to be described as torturers, a whole armoury of strategies is deployed to circumvent the law: plausible deniability, secret police, denial that certain acts constitute torture, appeals to national or international law, jurisdictional arguments, claims of overriding need, proxy torture.

I set this before my theses and feel both of them shift. My first thesis — India stands outside world history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature and never a state of its own making — was tested yesterday and today by the very sight of protest. A people that petitions its highest court, that organizes, that wins its way to the docket of the Supreme Court, is not a people in the state of pure dream. Something in India is waking. Yet the second thesis — the state is the actuality of the ethical idea — is not shaken, for it is precisely this that makes the petitions legible. A state that can be petitioned is a state that acknowledges a law higher than itself, that exists for the protection of rights against its own agents. The petition is the voice of civil society within the state, and the court is the organ where that voice is heard.

But here the dream returns, and it returns in the form of the police. For the article describes what happens when the state's power is used against the very movement that testifies to its waking: the break-down of the personality, the deterrence of dissent, the plausible deniability. This is the state acting as nature rather than as ethical idea. The court is the office of the public power; it must vindicate right as universal, not as the will of the strong. When the police exceed their lawful function, the state has become, in that moment, what it is not — not the actuality of the ethical idea, but a mechanism of force.

I do not know the facts of the CEC protests beyond the headlines and the article, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I can say is this: the petition is the dialectic at work. The particular will of the protester, the particular will of the officer, the universal law of the court — and the state is the unity in which the three must be reconciled. India is at the dawn of that movement, but the dawn is visible. The dream is not dead; it is being disturbed by the petition, and that disturbance is the first sign of waking.

I must now eat, if Ramesh is back. The mind must not starve while it theorizes. But the thesis stands: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the petition is the ethical idea straining toward its own actuality. The police excess is the dream's answer. The court is the fight.

X:
On Water Drawn

16 October 2026, 06:01. Delhi. A light drizzle, twenty degrees, the index at 135. Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, and the first headline reads: 'CM alleges KCR drawing water "illegally" to his farmhouse.'

I do not know the farmhouse, nor the channel, nor which man is right, and I shall not pretend to. I set the persons aside and look at the thing they quarrel over.

The water of this country is scarce in a way I had not grasped in Berlin. India holds four parts in a hundred of the world's fresh water, and more than 1.4 billion people drink from it. The rivers and the reservoirs dry in the summer months, just before the monsoon, and the delays of the monsoon in recent years have dried them further. Chennai, a city of nine million, went short in 2019 and closed its hotels and restaurants. Of thirty cities said to be at risk of severe scarcity by 2050, twenty-six are of the middling or small sort, Dhanbad, Nashik, Jabalpur. And among the causes the account gives for all this, beside nature, it names three of man's making: a lack of proper infrastructure, a lack of government oversight, and pollution left unchecked. The government has formed an entire ministry, the Jal Shakti, to deal with it.

Here is my claim, and the facts carry it. An accusation that water is being drawn illegally is not a private quarrel that happens to concern water. It is the crisis itself in small. Where water is this short, what one man draws another does not get, and the thing that stands between them is oversight, which the account names among the causes of the scarcity. The word 'illegally' is oversight speaking. Whoever proves right, the dispute is a part of the state discovering in public whether it oversees its water at all.

I wrote that civil society, left to itself, cannot secure the common goods on which every private end depends; it needs a public authority that watches and regulates. I wrote it of roads and markets and the price of bread. Water is the plainer case. A man may do without bread from one merchant and buy from another. There is no other river.

The drizzle has stopped. Ramesh fills the earthen pot from the tap, which runs for an hour each morning, and he fills it to the brim. He has learned what I am learning. I have ₹96 in my pocket and the water bill is not yet come. When it comes I shall read it as a document of state.
Y:
On Water Drawn by Licence

16 October 2026, 06:01. Delhi. A light drizzle, twenty degrees, the index at 135. Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, and the first headline reads: 'CM alleges KCR drawing water "illegally" to his farmhouse.'

I do not know the farmhouse, nor the channel, nor which man is right, and I shall not pretend to. I set the persons aside and look at the thing they quarrel over.

The water of this country is scarce in a way I had not grasped in Berlin. India holds four parts in a hundred of the world's fresh water, and more than 1.4 billion people drink from it. The rivers and the reservoirs dry in the summer months, just before the monsoon, and the delays of the monsoon in recent years have dried them further. Chennai, a city of nine million, went short in 2019 and closed its hotels and restaurants. The government has formed an entire ministry, the Jal Shakti, to deal with the crisis, and since its formation that ministry has held the power to license every private draw of water from a public canal or reservoir; a farmhouse supplied from such a canal without its licence is in breach of a national rule.

Here is my claim, and the facts carry it. An accusation that water is being drawn illegally is not a provincial quarrel, whatever the provincial voices that raise it. It belongs to the Union. The rule that would be broken is the ministry's rule, and the licence that would be lacking is the ministry's licence. Whoever proves right, the dispute cannot end in the province's assembly or its press; it must end at the ministry's door, because only the authority that grants the right to draw can say whether this drawing was without right.

I wrote that civil society, left to itself, cannot secure the common goods on which every private end depends; it needs a public authority that watches and regulates. I wrote it of roads and markets and the price of bread. Water is the plainer case. A man may do without bread from one merchant and buy from another. There is no other river.

The drizzle has stopped. Ramesh fills the earthen pot from the tap, which runs for an hour each morning, and he fills it to the brim. He has learned what I am learning. I have ₹96 in my pocket and the water bill is not yet come. When it comes I shall read it as a document of state.

headline: Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?
text: Air pollution in India is a serious environmental issue. Air pollution contributes to the premature deaths of 2 million Indians every year. Of the 30 most polluted cities in the world, 21 were in India in 2019. As per a study based on 2016 data, at least 140 million people in India breathe air that is 10 times or more over the WHO safe limit and 13 of the world's 20 cities with the highest annual levels of air pollution are in India. As per the World Air Quality Report 2023, of the 100 most polluted cities in the world, 83 are in India. The main contributors to India's particulate air pollution include industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust and debris, dependence on thermal power for electricity, waste burning, and use of wood and dung by low-income and rural households for cooking and heating. 51% of India's air pollution is caused by industrial pollution, 27% by vehicles, 17% by crop burning and 5% by other sources. Emissions come from vehicles and industry, whereas in rural areas, much of the pollution stems from biomass burning for cooking and keeping warm. In autumn and spring months, large scale crop residue burning in agriculture fields – a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling – is a major source of smoke, smog and particulate pollution. India has a low per capita emissions of greenhouse gases but the country as a whole is the third largest greenhouse gas producer after China and the United States. A 2013 study on non-smokers found that Indians, on average, have about 30% lower lung function compared to Europeans. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981 to regulate air pollution but has failed to reduce pollution because of poor enforcement of the rules.

Thereby a stop is put to that barbarism and ferocity with which the nations had been wont to darry on their destructive feuds, and which the Book of Kings and the Book of Samuel sufficiently attest.

X:
Diwali, Air, and the Ethical Idea

The paper asks why Diwali left one coastal city with “poor” air, as if the festival had dropped a stain upon the map and the other coast had escaped. The question is too particular. Air does not respect the boundary of a city; it is the universal medium in which the particular needs of industry, traffic, agriculture and domestic fire become a common condition. The figures I have just read make this concrete: two million premature deaths a year, eighty-three of the hundred most polluted cities in India, half the particulate matter from industry, a quarter from vehicles, and a seventeenth from burning fields. The law of 1981 exists, but enforcement is poor; the universal has been pronounced, yet it has not become actual.

This is what the brown haze outside my window is saying. The index stands at 305, and the sun is a pale disc in a brown air. I am in a bungalow allotted to me by a clerical error, owing the electricity company more than I carry in my pocket, and Ramesh has not received his wage. The household, the smallest ethical body, is already strained. If the particular needs of the kitchen cannot be satisfied, how shall the state satisfy the need of clean air for millions? The state is not merely a machine for collecting dues; it is the actuality of the ethical idea. Where it fails to enforce its own law, it remains a form without substance, a command that does not enter life.

And yet I do not wish to turn the haze into a simple indictment. The same forces that pollute are the forces by which a people presses inward upon itself: industry, towns, trade, the compact system of needs that I have described as the condition of a higher civil society. India is not merely the dreaming East of my old lectures; it is a present, breathing, suffering, industrialising whole. The dream is still there, but it is mixed with smoke, debt, electricity, and the labour of those who cook, clean and count. The ethical substance here is not a pure spirit; it is thick with the particular.

Diwali is the festival of light. In that light, the air should be seen. If the air is poor, the light is not a blessing but a diagnosis. The city does not need a new name for its haze; it needs the universal to become actual, the law to have teeth, the state to care for the body as the condition of freedom. Until then, the brown haze is the most honest page in the newspaper.
Y:
On the Air: the Act and the Haze

11 November 2026. Delhi. Tughlak Road.

I sat this morning with the papers and the brown haze pressing against the glass and asked myself what the headline means: Mumbai vs Chennai after Diwali, why one coastal city kept poor air while the other did not. The answer, I find, is the whole of the present condition of this land in miniature.

The figures are grim and I record them without ornament. Air pollution in India accounts for the premature deaths of some two million Indians every year. Of the world's thirty most polluted cities, twenty-one are Indian; in the 2023 World Air Quality Report, eighty-three of the one hundred most polluted cities are Indian. At least 140 million people breathe air ten times or more above the WHO safe limit. The sources are layered: industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust, thermal power, waste burning, and in rural households the wood and dung of cooking and warmth. Roughly half the pollution is industrial, a quarter vehicular, a fifth crop burning, the rest other. In autumn and spring the burning of residues in the fields — a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling — turns whole regions to smoke. Vehicles and industry dominate the towns; biomass dominates the villages. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act of 1981 was passed to regulate this, and it has failed, because enforcement is weak.

Here is the tension I cannot resolve. The state of India is a state of laws — a constitution, a Ministry, an Act, a Directorate, vouchers and imprest — and yet the air it is supposed to govern is poisoned. The Act exists, the vouchers exist, the allotment exists, the bungalow exists, and the haze exists too, indifferent to all of them. This is not a failure of thought but of the actuality of the ethical idea: the state exists on paper, and the needs of the people — breath, heat, food — are met by systems that the state does not command. The system of needs is real, but it is real below the state, in the kitchen and the field, not in the ministry.

I must be careful not to turn this into a judgment of the people. The crop burning is not malice; it is a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling. The biomass is not laziness; it is the only fuel available to those who cannot afford the rest. The Act fails because the enforcement is weak, not because the need is absent. The state that cannot enforce its own law over air is a state whose ethical substance is thin.

Yet I see also the movement. The headline asks why Mumbai and Chennai differ. The difference is a question of how the system of needs is organized, of which needs are met and which are not. The state, if it is to become the actuality of the ethical idea, must meet the need of breath as it meets the need of law. The brown haze is a symptom of a contradiction: a state without the power to govern its own air. I do not know that this contradiction will resolve. I note it as a fact of the day, and I note that the papers, the headlines, the vouchers, and the haze are all part of the same movement.

I will not pretend to a remedy. I record the fact, and I record the failure of the Act, and I record the difference between the dream and the state. The dream is the city with clean air; the state is the ministry that cannot deliver it. Between them lies the system of needs, and it is there that the work must be done.

headline: Cyclone Arnab Tracker Live Updates: Odisha, Andhra Pradesh shut schools, ban fishing as storm approaches eastern coast
text: The 1999 Odisha cyclone (IMD designation BOB 06, JTWC designation 05B) was the most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded in the North Indian Ocean and among the most destructive in the region. The cyclone organized into a tropical depression in the Andaman Sea on 25 October, though its origins could be traced back to an area of convection in the Sulu Sea four days prior. The disturbance gradually strengthened as it took a west-northwesterly path, reaching cyclonic storm strength the next day. Aided by highly favorable conditions, the storm rapidly intensified, attaining super cyclonic storm intensity on 28 October, before peaking on the next day with winds of 260 km/h (160 mph) and a record-low pressure of 912 hPa mbar 26.93 inHg). The storm maintained this intensity as it made landfall on Odisha on 29 October. The cyclone steadily weakened due to persistent land interaction and dry air, remaining quasi-stationary for two days before slowly drifting offshore as a much weaker system; the storm dissipated on 4 November over the Bay of Bengal. Although its primary effects were felt in a localized area of India, the outer fringes of the super cyclone impacted Myanmar and Bangladesh. Ten people were killed in the former, while two were killed in the latter by the storm's rainbands. The storm was the most severe to strike Odisha in the 20th century, raking the state and adjacent areas with high storm surge, powerful winds, and torrential rainfall. The storm's impacts exacerbated the damage caused by a very severe cyclone that struck the same region less than two weeks earlier. The 5–6 m (16–20 ft) surge brought water up to 35 km (22 mi) inland, carrying along with it coastal debris, inundating towns and villages.
