X:
Cyclone Arnab and the State’s Duty to the Particular

28 October 2026, 09:19, Delhi. The morning is clear but hazy, twenty-three degrees, the air quality index one hundred and sixty-two. I sat on the step where the hawker had thrown the papers. The headline that seized me was not the reunion of actors nor the counting of votes, but the tracker of Cyclone Arnab: schools shut, fishing banned, the storm approaching the eastern coast. I looked it up on my phone, and the phone gave me not Arnab but the memory of 1999: a super cyclone, winds of 260 km/h, pressure 912 hPa, a surge of five to six metres carried thirty-five kilometres inland.

I am struck less by the violence than by the administrative movement that the violence provokes. The state says: no school, no boat, no exposure. This is the universal taking up the particular. The child is not merely a family matter; the fisherman is not merely a private risk. The administration draws a line across the coast, and in that line there is something ethical, even if it is only the beginning of ethics. Nature does not distinguish between free and unfree; it drowns the temple, the bungalow, and the hut alike. The state, if it is to be more than a dream, must distinguish in time, must move before the water moves.

My old formula has been shaken. I had placed the East at the dawn, a spirit that dreams, its castes fixed like nature. But a state that shuts schools and bans fishing in the face of a cyclone is not merely dreaming. It is attempting to make the individual a citizen, to preserve the body that thought requires. Yet I do not call this the summit. The summit is not the mere preservation of life, but the free recognition of the universal as one’s own. Here the universal still speaks through fear, through command, through the tracker and the bulletin. It has not yet become the self-conscious freedom of a people who make their own state.

And yet the distinction matters. If the state can organize the particular against nature, it is no longer purely external. The storm is the test, not of the dream, but of the ethical substance: whether the administration can be more than a machine, and whether the people can be more than objects of its care. I am hungry, the house is empty, and Ramesh is absent; my body reminds me that freedom is not only thought. The haze outside chokes the eye, but the mind must keep its line. The cyclone will approach, or pass; the state will answer, or fail. I shall record the answer.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

28 October 2026, 09:45. Delhi. The papers lie on the step, and the headline that holds my attention is the one about the storm: Cyclone Arnab, live updates, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh shutting schools, banning fishing as it approaches the eastern coast. I looked it up on my phone, and the record is a grim one. The 1999 Odisha cyclone — BOB 06, 05B — organized in the Andaman Sea on 25 October, strengthened as it took a west-northwesterly path, attained super cyclonic storm intensity on 28 October, and peaked on the next day with winds of 260 km/h and a record-low pressure of 912 hPa. It made landfall on Odisha on 29 October. A 5–6 meter surge brought water up to 35 km inland, inundating towns and villages. It was the most severe cyclone to strike Odisha in the twentieth century, and it struck in the same season as a very severe cyclone less than two weeks earlier. Ten people were killed in Myanmar by its outer fringes, two in Bangladesh.

I set this against the bungalow on Tughlak Road and the papers on the step, and I am forced to see the Oriental world as I have always seen it, but with a new physical weight. The storm is the dream outside the dream. Nature here is not held in check by a state; it arrives, it dominates, it is survived by those who are nearest to it. The schools are shut, the fishing boats are banned from the water — a state of alert, a bureaucratic response, but a response that is itself a symptom of the weakness it tries to govern. In Berlin, a cholera or a flood would be met by a system of needs; here the storm is met by announcements, and the announcements are the whole of the state's effort.

Yet the tension is not simply between nature and state. It is between the dream of the East and the movement of world history. The storm is the given, the brute, the ungovernable; the schools and the fishing bans are the attempt to raise it into the universal. But the attempt is never complete, because the universal has not yet become the actual. India stands at the dawn of that history, and the storm is the dawn's hour: the light is coming, but the dark is still present, and the dark is strong.

I note, with a philosopher's dryness, that the 1999 cyclone was named BOB 06 and 05B, that it was tracked live, that it was a matter of records and bulletins. The storm is both a physical fact and a document. It is the Oriental world as it is recorded by the state that does not yet own it. My notes continue. The storm is on its way to the eastern coast; the schools are shut; the fishing is banned; and the dream of the East is, for the moment, a storm that has not yet passed.

headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency
text: The Emergency in India was a 21 month period from 1975 to 1977 when prime minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. Officially issued by president Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed under Article 352 of the Constitution of India because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", the Emergency were in effect from 25 June 1975 and ended on 21 March 1977. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. For much of the Emergency, most of Gandhi's political opponents were imprisoned and the press was censored. More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. During this time, a mass campaign for vasectomy was spearheaded by her son Sanjay Gandhi. The final decision to impose an emergency was proposed by Indira Gandhi, agreed upon by the President of India, and ratified by the Cabinet and the Parliament from July to August 1975. It was based on the rationale that there were imminent internal and external threats to the Indian state.

X:
The Emergency and the Law: On the Supreme Court's Bar on Illegal Detention

6 November 2026. Delhi.

The morning papers bring a headline that interests me more than the weather. The Supreme Court has barred illegal detention, and the lawyers have cited the Emergency in doing so. I sat with this for a while, and I confess that the words of the lawyers struck me, not as mere procedure, but as a moment in the life of a state.

To understand what an emergency is, one must understand what it suspends. The state, in its actuality, is the ethical idea made real: a body of law in which the particular wills of its members are subordinated to the universal will of the whole. When a government rules by decree, suspending elections, closing the press, and imprisoning opponents, it is not the state acting in its essence. It is the state in a state of crisis, reduced to sheer will — power in the service of a particular purpose rather than the universal one. The Emergency of 1975–77, as the lawyers invoke it, was precisely such a suspension. The decree is the state's actuality denied: the universal subordinated to the particular will of one man.

And yet the lawyers cite it — not as a triumph, but as a warning. They say: this has happened here; it must not happen again. The Supreme Court, barring illegal detention, acts as the guardian of the law's supremacy. The particular — the lawyer, the petitioner, the court — serves the universal: the rule of law. This is the movement I have always loved: the particular rising into the universal, the individual case becoming the instrument of a principle.

But I must be honest with myself. I came to Delhi with a fixed conviction: that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature and its many gods, and never a state of its own making. I have sat with that conviction for weeks, and it has not dissolved. But this headline troubles it. For the lawyers who cited the Emergency are not dreaming; they are citing a law, arguing from a statute, invoking a precedent. This is not the oriental dream. This is the Germanic movement — the idea of law as the actuality of freedom — operating in a city that does not resemble my Berlin at all. The dream and the law coexist here, as they do everywhere, but in a different proportion. Perhaps my conviction is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Perhaps India is at the dawn of the movement, and this headline is a sign of the dawn — not a state of its own making, but a state in the making, struggling to become what it is not yet.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. In India, that idea is being struggled toward. The Supreme Court's bar on illegal detention is a small victory for the idea. The Emergency is a large defeat. The lawyers who cited it are the particular; the rule of law is the universal. The movement is not complete. It is not yet the summit. But it is moving.

I shall not pretend that I understand this fully. I am a German philosopher in a bungalow on Tughlak Road, writing in a brown haze, with the air quality index at 290 and a caretaker waiting for his wage. I am a particular. But the headline is a universal, and I try to think it. The law is not the state's actuality; the state is the law's actuality. And the lawyers, citing the Emergency, are saying: the law must be actual, even when the state is tempted to suspend it.

I shall return to the vouchers. The dhobi is due on Saturday. The body demands its fuel, but the mind must continue its work. The Emergency is not the end of the state; it is a moment of crisis. The Supreme Court is not the summit; it is a particular. But the movement is real, and I shall record it.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East, sitting 4

6 November 2026, Delhi, 09:10. The air is a brown haze, and the papers lie on the verandah as if the state had left a message and then withdrawn. Ramesh is present, and asks for ₹8,000, the wage for cooking. I have ₹1,286. I say nothing yet. The demand is particular, urgent, and it makes me feel the emptiness of a universal claim that cannot produce bread. I have not eaten since yesterday; the body is a mechanism waiting for fuel, while the mind is occupied with a headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency.

Before writing, I read on my phone an account of the Emergency in India, 1975 to 1977: a state of emergency declared by the prime minister, Indira Gandhi, under Article 352 of the Constitution, ratified by Cabinet and Parliament, allowing rule by decree, the suspension of civil liberties, the imprisonment of political opponents and journalists, and censorship. More than one hundred thousand persons were said to have been imprisoned. I do not know how to place these facts in my system except as a later and more concrete form of what I knew in theory: the state can become a power that swallows the individual, and law can become the instrument of its own exception.

Yet the present sentence is not merely a record of power. The Supreme Court bars illegal detention, and lawyers cite the Emergency. This is a movement. The abuse returns into the courtroom as a warning. The particular fear of the detained, the particular memory of the imprisoned, has become a universal argument before the judges. The state is not simply the will of the moment; it is the ethical idea in process, and its process includes the correction of its own excesses. A constitution is grown, not made; here it seems to grow by remembering its wound.

This shakes my old note that India stands outside the movement of world history. I do not abandon the thesis, but I cannot keep it as a closed door. The dream has produced a court, a bar, a constitutional article, a political opposition, and a public argument about liberty. Whether this is the beginning of a state of its own making, or only the administration of a state made under other names, I cannot yet say. What I can say is that the particular has entered the universal: Ramesh’s unpaid wage, the brown haze, the court’s bar, and the memory of the Emergency are not separate facts. They are one movement of reason in an age that does not yet know itself.

headline: Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance
text: The Government of Punjab or locally as the State Government, is the supreme governing authority of the Indian state of Punjab, India and its 23 districts. It consists of an executive, led by the Governor of Punjab, a judiciary and a legislative branch Punjab State. Like other states in India, the head of state of Punjab is the Punjab Governor, appointed by the President of India on the advice of the Central government. The post of governor is largely ceremonial. The Chief Minister of Punjab is the head of government and is vested with most of the executive powers. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab, and houses the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and the secretariat. Chandigarh also serves as the capital of Haryana, and is a union territory of India. The Punjab & Haryana High Court, located in Chandigarh, has jurisdiction over the whole state. The present Punjab Legislative Assembly is unicameral, consisting of 117 Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA). Its term is 5 years, unless sooner dissolved.

X:
The Governor Who Dots the I

25 November 2026. Tughlak Road. Mostly clear, hazy, eighteen degrees.

Two parties in Punjab, the BJP and the SAD, have announced an alliance for the assembly polls. I know these parties only by their initials, and the paper gives me nothing of their terms. What I read about the government they hope to form taught me more.

The Governor of Punjab is the head of state, appointed by the President on the advice of the centre, and his post is largely ceremonial. The Chief Minister holds most of the executive power. A hundred and seventeen members sit in a single chamber for five years.

'Ceremonial' is said with a shrug, as if the office were an ornament. I lectured otherwise about my own monarch. In a developed constitution the prince does little more than say 'I will' and dot the i; the content of the decision is prepared by ministers who answer for it. Yet the dot is not nothing. It is the point at which the deliberations of particular men become the decision of the state, the moment of pure subjectivity by which a whole becomes a self. An appointed governor is not a hereditary prince, and I will not pretend the two are alike. But the shape is recognisable: someone must stand for the whole without being one of the parties that fight over it.

Which brings me to the parties. Alliances are the arithmetic of factions: two particular interests add themselves together to make a majority and call the sum a programme. I always preferred that a people be represented through its estates and corporations, through the real articulations of its life, rather than through associations formed for the purpose of winning. An alliance announced before an election tells the voter which particulars have agreed to combine. It does not yet tell him what universal they serve. That he learns afterwards, if at all.

The note adds a curiosity. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab and of Haryana, and is itself a union territory: a city that houses two governments and is governed by a third. I read my own file in the same light. Shri Hegde now asks that the allotment stand in his name, with me on record as his guest. The bungalow would be his, the study in which I write would be lent to me, and the Directorate would stand over us both.

I find, to my surprise, that I object less than I expected. A guest has standing too; hospitality is a relation of right, not a charity. The shelf this morning warns against the freedom that flees every content as a limit, the freedom of the void. To be recorded somewhere, even as a guest, is better than to be no one in a file.
Y:
The Alliance on the Step

The papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them, and the headline that holds the morning is this: Punjab Assembly polls — BJP-SAD announce alliance. I sit with it a while, in the haze, and I try to read it as a movement rather than a news item. A movement is what I am for. A newspaper is only a snapshot; the truth of a thing is in what it is turning into.

What the Punjab facts tell me, from the page I read on my phone, is that the state is not a single thing but a structure of particular powers. The Governor is largely ceremonial, appointed on the advice of the Central government; the Chief Minister is the head of government and holds most of the executive power. Chandigarh houses the Vidhan Sabha and the secretariat; the Punjab and Haryana High Court has jurisdiction over the whole state. The Assembly is unicameral, 117 members, a term of five years unless sooner dissolved. Here is a state that is real but thin: a head of state who governs little, a head of government who governs all, a legislature that can be dissolved at will. The constitution is grown, as I have always said, not made; yet it can be dissolved, and the dissolve is part of the life of the state, not its death.

Now the alliance. The BJP is the party of the nation — the universal will of the Hindu-majority middle, the party that speaks for India as a whole. The SAD, the Shiromani Akali Dal, is the party of a particular region, a particular community, a particular history. An alliance between them is a moment in which two particular wills resolve into a temporary universal: a coalition that will govern 117 seats. In Hegel's terms, the particular abolishes itself in the universal. Here the particular is not a caste or a family but a party, and the universal is not the ethical idea but the state of a particular province. Still, the movement is the same: particular wills, aware of their own finitude, allying to become a government. The alliance is not a miracle; it is the state being actualized through the struggle of its particular organs.

I must be honest with myself: this is the first time in my life that I have watched a state assemble itself the way I have always described it — not as a dream but as a machine of particular interests, negotiating, bargaining, allying, governing. India, I have said, dreams; its castes are fixed like nature; its many gods are a multiplicity without a state of its own. And yet here is a state, with a Chief Minister, an Assembly, a High Court, a capital, and a coalition that is being formed in real time. The theses shake. Not because they are false but because they are incomplete. India is at the dawn of world history, I said; perhaps the dawn is earlier than I understood, or the sun is already rising.

The haze outside is 164, a brown fog that mirrors the opacity of the administrative logic I have been fighting in the Directorate. The papers are on the step. The recital at the Habitat Centre is in the evening. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens to clear this from my head, and then I will go to the Directorate, and then to the recital, and then I will return and reflect. The alliance will announce itself again tomorrow. The state will turn. The dream will wake.

text: The Republic of India and the United States established diplomatic relations in 1947 following Indian independence. Relations between the two countries have developed in areas including defense, trade, technology, education and energy. The two countries have also cooperated on regional and international issues, while differences have remained over trade, energy policy and other matters. In early 2026, energy policy became a significant issue in India–United States relations. The United States sought changes to India's purchases of Russian oil, while India considered the economic and logistical implications of changing its sources of crude oil. The United States and India announced a trade agreement in February 2026. President Donald Trump said that India had agreed to stop purchasing Russian oil and increase imports from the United States and potentially Venezuela, alongside reductions in tariffs on Indian goods. Indian officials said that energy security and diversification remained priorities and that refiners would require time to complete previously arranged Russian oil shipments. Reuters reported that India's imports of Russian oil had declined in January 2026 amid the trade negotiations, while Indian energy officials indicated that the country was broadening its sources of crude oil.

X:
On the Verbalization of the State: Notes on the US-India Deal

21 October 2026, 07:15. Delhi. The air is hazy, the index 180, the temperature a deceptive 20 degrees. I have sat with the newspaper on my lap, the headline regarding Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the US-India deal staring back at me with a kind of administrative absurdity.

The text reads: ‘On US-India deal… it’s down to certain words, phrases… We are weeks from finalising it… 99% of the work is done.’

I am struck by the mechanism. A treaty, which ought to be the expression of the rational will of states, is described as a matter of 'words' and 'phrases.' This is the triumph of the negative over the positive. The substance of the agreement—the ethical and political reality it is meant to embody—is reduced to its linguistic shell. The '99% of the work' suggests that the structural, rational framework is complete, yet the final 1% is a stumbling block of mere signification. 

In my notes on the Ethical Substance, I argued that the state is grown, not made. A constitution or a treaty is not a contract in the mechanical sense, where parties merely exchange signatures. It is the actuality of the ethical idea. Yet here, in this modern diplomatic maneuvering, we see the ethical idea caught in the trap of externalization. The 'words' are the external form, the particular, that must be reconciled with the universal intent. If the 'words' and 'phrases' are the stumbling block, it means the spirit of the agreement has not yet fully penetrated its own expression. It is a moment of alienation: the state’s will is trapped in the medium of language, struggling to achieve self-recognition through its own utterances.

This resonates with my observation of the 'dream' of the East. In the Oriental world, the spirit is often lost in the immediate, the natural, the undifferentiated. Here, in the diplomatic sphere of the 'Germanic' or modern world, the spirit is lost in the abstract, the formal, the verbal. The 'certain words' are the new 'castes'—fixed, unchangeable, and yet supposedly free. The negotiators are like the castes, bound by the forms they use, unable to transcend them to reach the rational unity of the state.

I wonder if this '99%' is a lie of civil society, a way to mask the lack of substantive agreement. Or is it a genuine moment of the dialectic, where the universal (the deal) must suffer the pain of the particular (the words) to become actual? I suspect the latter. The 'finalizing' is the act of sublation (Aufhebung), where the tension between the intent and the expression is resolved. But it is a fragile resolution, dependent on the 'certain words' being chosen correctly. It is not a growth of spirit, but a tightening of a knot.

The hazy air outside mirrors this opacity. The truth is not clear; it is suspended in the phrase. I must wait for the 'finalising,' but I suspect the '99%' is the only part that is real. The 1% is the ghost, the Hegel/Hegde error, the mistake that allows the spirit to recognize itself. Without the error, there is no recognition. Without the 'certain words,' there is no deal. The dream of the East is static; the dream of the West is verbal. Both are dreams, because neither has fully achieved the ethical substance of the state. They are both in the process of becoming, or rather, of trying to be, what they are not yet. The '99%' is the body; the '1%' is the soul. They must be joined, or the body remains a corpse, and the soul a phantom.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026, 06:40. Delhi.

The papers lie on the step, and one headline has kept me up past my usual hour. The Secretary of State speaks of a deal between the United States and India: weeks from finalising, 99 per cent of the work done, down to certain words, certain phrases. I read it three times, and I cannot stop thinking about what is left in that 1 per cent, and about the strange confidence of a world-state that treats a treaty as a matter of drafting.

I had thought, this morning, that the Oriental dream was a matter of gods and castes, of a spirit that dreams and never grows a state of its own making. The papers now suggest something else: that this dream is not idle. It is being negotiated. It is being bought and sold, clause by clause, by powers that hold their own ethical substances and believe them to be the measure of all things. The Oriental is not outside history; he is being hurried along it. Whether that is progress or merely commerce is the question I cannot yet answer.

Consider the structure of the sentence. The work is 99 per cent done. What remains is language. It is as if the substance were already in hand, and what was missing were only the words to give it shape. This is the cunning of reason in its most mundane form: the idea that the real is the written. In Berlin I would have said the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, that it is grown, not made. Here, the state appears as a text under negotiation, and the ethical idea as a phrase awaiting final approval.

The 1 per cent is not nothing. Words are the medium in which freedom moves. A clause can bind or release; a phrase can name a right or erase it. To leave the decisive work to the last words is to leave the ethical substance in the hands of those who draft. I do not know whether this is a defect of the Indian dream or of the Western method. I suspect it is both: the dream of a spirit that has not yet grown its own state, and the method of a power that treats every state as a text.

I must mark what is speculation. I have not read the treaty. I have not met the Secretary of State. I know only the headline and the confidence of the phrase. What follows is my interpretation, not a report.

Still, the tension is real. On one side, the Oriental dream: castes fixed like nature, gods undifferentiated, a history that is traffic rather than passage. On the other, the Germanic state: grown, rational, the actuality of freedom. The deal between two powers, one of them outside the movement and one within it, is a small spectacle of that tension. The Oriental is being drawn into the movement, not by its own growth but by the commerce of the Germanic world. Is that the dawn of history, or merely the arrival of a buyer?

I return to the step. The papers are limp in the haze. The air quality is grim. The sun will come. I will eat, I will walk, I will write again. The dream remains, and the deal remains, and the 1 per cent remains.

text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). X:
The Gold and the Small Change

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The index is 236 and the haze lies on the garden like dust on a ledger. The paper reports that 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees have been seized in raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh.

The figures are meant to astonish, and they do. A man's house full of metal. But I distrust the astonishing in matters of state, and I went to read what is known of corruption in this country as a whole.

It is this. In a study of 2020, thirty-nine in every hundred Indians said they had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done within the preceding twelve months. In the index of perceived corruption released this year, India scored 39 of a possible 100 and stood 91st of 182 countries, and its score has moved only between 36 and 41 since the index took its present form in 2012. Officials siphon money from welfare schemes, from the rural employment guarantee and the rural health mission. Truckers pay at police and regulatory stops along the highways, billions of rupees a year. Money is said to be hidden in Swiss banks.

Here is my claim, and it rests on these facts alone. The seizure misleads by its very splendour. Corruption, as these facts describe it, is not a hoard; it is a habit. It is the small payment made by two in five to have an ordinary thing done, the note handed over at the checkpost, the share taken from a scheme meant for the poor. A thing so spread through the ordinary cannot be measured by what is taken from one man's cupboards, and the proof is the score, which has scarcely stirred in thirteen years. The gold in Madhya Pradesh tells me about one officer. The condition lies in the small change.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, not an exception. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it: not gold, but the expectation of a coin.
Y:
The Gold and the Revenue Office

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The index is 236 and the haze lies on the garden like dust on a ledger. The paper reports that 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees have been seized in raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh.

The figures are meant to astonish, and they do. A man's house full of metal. But I distrust the astonishing in matters of state, and I went to read what is known of corruption in this country as a whole.

It is this. In a study of 2020, thirty-nine in every hundred Indians said they had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done within the preceding twelve months, and the same study found that more than half of those bribes were paid at offices of land and revenue, where an officer's signature decides who holds a field. In the index of perceived corruption released this year, India scored 39 of a possible 100 and stood 91st of 182 countries, and its score has moved only between 36 and 41 since 2012. Officials siphon money from welfare schemes. Truckers pay at stops along the highways.

Here is my claim, and it rests on these facts. The seizure does not mislead; it shows the type. Corruption here is not spread evenly through the state; it gathers where the state grants title to the earth. Where the bribe buys a field, it is not small change, and what is paid over years in such an office does not stay in a pocket. It becomes metal in a cupboard. A hoard like this one is the form that this corruption takes when it accumulates, and the score that has scarcely stirred in thirteen years is the sign of an office whose habits have not changed.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, with its own seat. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it, at its edge: and at its centre, the gold.

headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency
text: The Emergency in India was a 21 month period from 1975 to 1977 when prime minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. Officially issued by president Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed under Article 352 of the Constitution of India because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", the Emergency were in effect from 25 June 1975 and ended on 21 March 1977. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. For much of the Emergency, most of Gandhi's political opponents were imprisoned and the press was censored. More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. During this time, a mass campaign for vasectomy was spearheaded by her son Sanjay Gandhi. The final decision to impose an emergency was proposed by Indira Gandhi, agreed upon by the President of India, and ratified by the Cabinet and the Parliament from July to August 1975. It was based on the rationale that there were imminent internal and external threats to the Indian state.

X:
The Exception and Its Memory

6 November 2026. Tughlak Road, morning; brown haze, 290 on the index.

The Supreme Court, the paper says, has barred illegal detention, and the lawyers before it spoke of the Emergency. I read what that was. For twenty-one months from June 1975 the Prime Minister ruled by decree under a proclamation of internal disturbance. Elections were put off, the press was censored, more than a hundred thousand opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned, and a campaign of vasectomy was driven by her son. The President signed it; the cabinet and parliament ratified it some weeks afterwards.

I must be honest about my own doctrine before I judge anyone else's. I taught that sovereignty is hidden in peaceful times, when each department and estate goes about its own business, and that it shows itself in distress, when the particular spheres are called back into the whole. I do not think a state is obliged to perish politely. A constitution that cannot act in danger is a paper constitution.

So my objection is not to the exception as such. It is to what the exception was used for. Sovereignty in danger means the universal gathering itself against a threat to the whole. Here, as far as one paragraph lets me see, the threat was named by the very person whose position it threatened, and the remedy fell upon opponents, upon printers, upon the bodies of the poor. That is not the idealism of the state. It is a particular will dressed in the state's coat. The difference is whether the extraordinary power serves the constitution or the constitution is made to serve the power.

And note the order of events. The proclamation came first; parliament's consent came after. In a rational constitution the legislative estates may be slow, but they are not an afterthought.

What pleases me in this morning's report is not the verdict, which I have not read, but the citation. The lawyers did not argue from abstract rights of man. They argued from a remembered wrong of their own people. That is how a constitution grows: not from the drawing board but from what a nation has suffered and resolved not to suffer again. 1977 has become a precedent in the deepest sense, a part of the ethical substance that the court can appeal to as one appeals to a custom.

I write this with twelve hundred rupees in my purse while Ramesh asks for eight thousand. The state's arithmetic and mine are both in a kind of emergency. Neither of us may simply suspend what we owe.
Y:
The Emergency and the Law: On the Supreme Court's Bar on Illegal Detention

6 November 2026. Delhi.

The morning papers bring a headline that interests me more than the weather. The Supreme Court has barred illegal detention, and the lawyers have cited the Emergency in doing so. I sat with this for a while, and I confess that the words of the lawyers struck me, not as mere procedure, but as a moment in the life of a state.

To understand what an emergency is, one must understand what it suspends. The state, in its actuality, is the ethical idea made real: a body of law in which the particular wills of its members are subordinated to the universal will of the whole. When a government rules by decree, suspending elections, closing the press, and imprisoning opponents, it is not the state acting in its essence. It is the state in a state of crisis, reduced to sheer will — power in the service of a particular purpose rather than the universal one. The Emergency of 1975–77, as the lawyers invoke it, was precisely such a suspension. The decree is the state's actuality denied: the universal subordinated to the particular will of one man.

And yet the lawyers cite it — not as a triumph, but as a warning. They say: this has happened here; it must not happen again. The Supreme Court, barring illegal detention, acts as the guardian of the law's supremacy. The particular — the lawyer, the petitioner, the court — serves the universal: the rule of law. This is the movement I have always loved: the particular rising into the universal, the individual case becoming the instrument of a principle.

But I must be honest with myself. I came to Delhi with a fixed conviction: that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature and its many gods, and never a state of its own making. I have sat with that conviction for weeks, and it has not dissolved. But this headline troubles it. For the lawyers who cited the Emergency are not dreaming; they are citing a law, arguing from a statute, invoking a precedent. This is not the oriental dream. This is the Germanic movement — the idea of law as the actuality of freedom — operating in a city that does not resemble my Berlin at all. The dream and the law coexist here, as they do everywhere, but in a different proportion. Perhaps my conviction is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Perhaps India is at the dawn of the movement, and this headline is a sign of the dawn — not a state of its own making, but a state in the making, struggling to become what it is not yet.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. In India, that idea is being struggled toward. The Supreme Court's bar on illegal detention is a small victory for the idea. The Emergency is a large defeat. The lawyers who cited it are the particular; the rule of law is the universal. The movement is not complete. It is not yet the summit. But it is moving.

I shall not pretend that I understand this fully. I am a German philosopher in a bungalow on Tughlak Road, writing in a brown haze, with the air quality index at 290 and a caretaker waiting for his wage. I am a particular. But the headline is a universal, and I try to think it. The law is not the state's actuality; the state is the law's actuality. And the lawyers, citing the Emergency, are saying: the law must be actual, even when the state is tempted to suspend it.

I shall return to the vouchers. The dhobi is due on Saturday. The body demands its fuel, but the mind must continue its work. The Emergency is not the end of the state; it is a moment of crisis. The Supreme Court is not the summit; it is a particular. But the movement is real, and I shall record it.

headline: NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused
text: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is an autonomous body under Department of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education of India. It was established in November 2017 to conduct entrance examinations, admissions and recruitment. As of 2025, it no longer conducts recruitment examinations. The agency is responsible for conducting numerous national-level exams for admission and fellowship in higher educational institutions related to engineering, medicine, management, research and pharmacy. Critics have also questioned the NTA's management, saying it lacks transparency and public accountability. Because of these problems, many court cases have been filed against it, and the government has announced reviews and possible reforms to improve its functioning.

X:
On the Leak: NEET and the State of Wants

19 November 2026, Delhi.

The papers this morning carry a headline that has nothing of the poetry of the Lodhi domes and everything of the clerk's desk: the Delhi court orders the framing of charges against fourteen accused in the NEET paper leak case. The National Testing Agency, an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education, exists to conduct the examinations by which the students of this country are admitted to the universities of the country. It is, in effect, the state's instrument of selection: a machine that converts the ambition of a young man into a place in a college, and the place into a life. It has been, in the reports, repeatedly controversial: paper leaks, unfair grace marks, technical and administrative problems at examination centres, court cases, announced reviews and possible reforms. The court now moves to frame charges. The state, in its way, is doing what it does: it is converting a want into a case, and a case into an order.

I find this instructive, and I find it troubling, and I think the two are the same. The examination is a system of wants in the precise sense of my Philosophy of Right: the student's want for admission, the family's want for a stable future, the university's want for order, the state's want for a population sorted into its stations. In a good examination, the want is satisfied by work: the candidate sits, the paper holds, the result is a measure of what the candidate has done. The leak is the want satisfied by fraud. The candidate who has not worked enters through the back door, and the candidate who has worked is cheated of his place. The system of wants is corrupted not by the absence of wants but by the substitution of one means for another. The court's order is the administration of justice attempting to restore the legitimate means.

Here I must be honest with myself, as I have not always been. I have written that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, that a constitution is grown and not made, that education begins with obedience and that the pupil must first learn to follow before his own judgment is worth anything. All of that is true as a description of the Germanic world, where the state is the actuality of the ethical idea and the exam is one of its instruments. But I am writing this in Delhi, in a bungalow allotted by mistake, in a country whose history I have described as a dream, and I find the description straining. A leak is not an Oriental dream; it is a modern administrative failure, and it is precisely the kind of failure that the ethical idea is supposed to cure. The state here is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the attempt, and the attempt is visible, and the attempt is failing in the small, clerical ways that a leak is a small, clerical failure.

The court's order is a small, clerical failure of a different kind: the administration of justice in its most literal form. It is the state at its most honest, perhaps, when it is not dreaming but framing charges. I do not know the facts of the case, and I must not pretend to. I know the headline, and the phone's account of the NTA, and the fact of the fourteen accused. What I know is that the system of wants is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea here, and that the distance between the two is exactly the distance between the dream and the state.

I will return to the file at the Directorate this afternoon. The file is in the hands of bureaucracy, which moves slowly, and the leak is in the hands of the court, which moves with its own slowness. Both are the state attempting to convert a want into a case. Both are the state attempting to become the actuality of the ethical idea. I shall watch, and I shall think, and I shall not pretend that the dream is the state.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

19 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi.

The headline on the front page: "NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused." I read the details on the device Ramesh calls a phone. The National Testing Agency, established in 2017, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education. It is the gatekeeper to the profession, the universal credential that allows the particular individual to enter the system of wants as a doctor or engineer.

The leak is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular will of the corrupt, selling what belongs to the universal. But the court's order is the moment of the state's actuality. The state does not merely dream; it judges. The "framing of charges" is the administration of justice, the protection of the right of the honest candidate against the fraud of the dishonest.

I thought of my own file at the Directorate. It is also in the hands of the state. But my case is a friction of the clerical, the Hegde/Hegel error. The NEET case is a friction of the ethical, the violation of the law itself. The state acts more decisively against the latter than the former. This confirms that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but its movement is uneven. It is swift where the ethical order is threatened (the exam integrity), and slow where it is merely administrative (my allotment).

The 14 accused are particulars. They will be sublated into the universal judgment. Their freedom is the freedom of the negative, the freedom to act against the law, which the law must negate to preserve itself. This is the dialectic of right. The state is not a dream; it is the power that negates the particular corruption. The "dream of the East" is not the state, but the corruption that the state must police.

I must keep this in mind for the talk at the IIC. The state is alive. It bites.

X:
Beer, Curd and the Multiplication of Needs

17 October 2026. Saturday, a little after six. Fog, and a brown light at the window. The dhobi is paid, three hundred rupees; Ramesh is about the house.

Beer sales, says the paper, have risen by more than forty per cent in six months. I went to my telephone for the history of the thing and was given instead a page on the Indian kitchen, which is perhaps the better answer. A kitchen tells you what a people permits itself.

What I read: that the Hindu often refuses beef, the Muslim pork, and the Jain refuses even the egg and the root, keeping only milk and grain and leaf. Here religion does not wait in the church for Sunday. It stands at the stove. The prohibition reaches into the pot and divides one man's dinner from his neighbour's. In Swabia my mother's table was Lutheran only in its grace; the dumplings were for everyone.

Now set beside this a forty per cent rise in beer. I edited a newspaper in Bamberg and I know what Franconian brewers are; beer there is not an event but a climate. Here it seems to be an event. Who is drinking it? The paper does not tell me, and I will not invent the drinker. But I can say what kind of movement it is. In my lectures on right I described civil society as the place where needs multiply: a want is divided into many wants, each with its own article and its own shop, and men learn to desire what others desire because others desire it. That is not yet freedom. It is Willkür, caprice, the freedom to choose among goods.

Still, caprice is the first crack in a wall. The table governed by birth says: this you are, therefore this you eat. The shop says: this you can pay for, therefore this you may have. The second is shallower, but it treats the buyer as a person and not as a member of a caste. So the beer is a small solvent. It does not raise anyone to the universal; it only loosens the particular.

I have written before that India dreams with its castes fixed like nature. The pot and the bottle make me less sure the fixing is complete. Nature does not sell forty per cent more of anything in six months. Something is moving, and I do not yet know whether it moves towards a freer ethical life or only towards a larger market.

Ramesh, I note, has offered nothing about it, and I have not asked him. The parathas from the morning are there if I ask. I have not yet asked for those either.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

17 October 2026, 06:30. Delhi.

The papers on the verandah carry a headline that I keep turning over: beer on a new high, sales up over forty per cent in the first six months of the financial year. I read it twice, then the other two — Canada's new immigration rules favouring Indian professionals with local work experience; the Chief Minister invited to Navaratri at Srisailam — and then sat with the beer.

The East dreams, I have written, and its dreams are fixed like nature: caste, gods, festivals. Yet here is the market of desire, rising by forty per cent in half a year. The dream has acquired a pulse. The body — the material organism — is restless, and the restlessness is traded, taxed, and counted. I am forced to ask whether this is the dawn of history or only the growth of a need.

I think it is the latter, and I should say why. Beer is an answer to the body, not to the spirit. It is the system of needs — civil society, in my terminology — the moment in which the particular wants and the universal market meet. Desire is real, and it is universal; but the system of needs is not the state. It is the intermediate moment, the realm in which the particular man is absorbed into the universal without yet being free. In Berlin, the same article would read as the pulse of industry, commerce, the civilisation of the market — a stage through which the ethical idea passes on its way to the state. Here, the numbers are rising, but the ethical substance has not grown. The caste remains fixed; the festival remains a festival; the god remains a god. The body wants, and the market sells to the body. That is not freedom. It is sustenance with a pulse.

I note the contrast with my own old teaching. In the Philosophy of Mind, the sublime divinity to which the work of art succeeds in giving expression is one in which the spectator finds himself at home, satisfied and liberated: the vision and consciousness of free spirit. Beer gives no such vision. It gives thirst quenched. The beer is a material organism, not a spiritual one. The headline counts cases and bottles; it does not count recognition.

And yet — here is the tension the papers force upon me — the rise in beer sales is also a sign that the East is not simply passive. It is not a landscape of tombs; it is a market. The Canada headline is a sharper shock: immigration rules that favour Indian professionals with local work experience. Here is the East, not as dream but as labour, as migrant, as professional — a people moving into the free world of commerce and law. I have written that India stands outside the movement of history. The papers suggest that the East is being pulled into the movement, not by its own ethical substance but by the traffic of profit and need. The dream is leaking — not into freedom, but into consumption.

The Chief Minister's invitation to Navaratri at Srisailam is the other pole: the festival, the faith, the devotion that bind the many gods into a single rhythm. The Navaratri is a festival of the body and the spirit together, but it is not a constitution. It is not a state. It is a dream that repeats itself.

So the papers give me three things: a rising market, a migrating professional class, a festival. The market and the migration are the East's encounter with the West's movement; the festival is the East's refusal to leave itself. I remain unshaken in the second thesis — the state is the actuality of the ethical idea — but the first thesis is shaken. India is not a world standing still outside history; it is a world being drawn into history by the very needs that the dream had held in place. The dream is not dead. It is being priced.

I will return to the vouchers, but I have set down this tension. The beer is not the state. The beer is the system of needs. The state is still to come, or still to be grown — and I do not know whether it will come from within the dream or from outside it, by the traffic of profit, by the migration of professionals, by the market's relentless arithmetic. That is the question the papers leave me with.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East — Cyclone Arnab and the State

29 October 2026. Delhi.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East (notes; continued)

The papers on the verandah today carry a headline that does not resolve into the universal: “Very severe cyclone Arnab crosses Andhra coast, weakens into severe cyclonic storm: IMD | LIVE.” A storm with a name, live-tracked, weakening as it weakens. Over a lakh evacuated. Odisha bracing for heavy rain. Rajnath Singh and the U.S. defence pact, reviewed in the same morning. Two worlds in one sheet: the state of the world, and the world’s own weather.

I must say at once that this headline unsettles me more than any I have read in my days here. A cyclone is not a philosophical category. It is not a caste, a creed, a constitution. It is a force of nature that does not consult the ethical idea, does not recognize the state, does not care for the allotment of bungalows. And yet it crosses the Andhra coast and is weakened by it—the coast absorbs, the storm diminishes. The earth is patient with the state; the state is not patient with the earth. India, which I have long read as a dream of fixed nature—castes as given, gods as many, a people outside the movement of world history—turns out to be also a country of cyclone, of evacuation, of live bulletins. The dream has weather. The dream has a body that can be battered.

This is the shaking I feel. In my notes I have written that India stands at the dawn of world history, outside its movement, a spirit that dreams. But a cyclone is not a dream. It is a fact that arrives. The evacuees are not citizens in the Germanic sense—they are not yet rational subjects of a state that thinks itself free. Yet they are also not mere nature; they are moved by an administration, counted, moved by the state’s own machinery of evacuation. The state, here, is not the actuality of the ethical idea as I have defined it, but something more immediate and more desperate: a system of needs that must be fed while the storm approaches.

Yet the second headline keeps me honest. Rajnath Singh and the U.S. defence pact: the state, even in a live storm, is engaged in the work of the universal—alliances, negotiations, the coordination of powers. This is the state as actuality: not the dream, not the caste, not the storm, but the rational organization that takes in the particular and makes it serve the whole. The state does not abolish the cyclone. It responds to it. It evacuates. It reviews defence pacts. It does not dream; it works.

So I hold my thesis, and I do not shake it. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But I see now that this is not a thesis to be stated with the confidence of a Berlin lecture. It is a thesis to be tested in the rain, in the evacuation, in the headline that says “weakens” and “LIVE.” India is not the dream outside history. It is the dream, battered, and the state, responding. The two are not separate. They are the same country, and the same country is still not free in the Germanic sense. But it is working. It is being.

I must go in. Ramesh has tea. The papers are damp. The drizzle is on the tiles. The cyclone is somewhere south, and I am somewhere north, and the world is a single fabric that neither of us can see whole. I shall continue the notes. The notes are the work of the spirit. The storm is the work of the earth. I am a guest in both.
Y:
Notes on the Cyclone and the Porous Nature of the Oriental Dream

29 October 2026, 09:10. Delhi. The air quality index is 238, a brown suspension that chokes the clarity of the mind as it does the lungs. The drizzle falls on the verandah tiles, a minor meteorological phenomenon, yet it interrupts the stillness of the morning. Ramesh has brought the tea; the papers are spread before me, damp at the edges. The headline reads: “Very severe cyclone Arnab crosses Andhra coast, weakens into severe cyclonic storm: IMD | LIVE.”

I am struck by the name. Arnab. It is a local name, drawn from the Sanskrit *arṇava*, the ocean. The storm is named after the very element that destroys it. This is not the arbitrary naming of a Germanic system, where a cyclone might be given a neutral or foreign label to distance it from the human sphere. Here, the particular event is embedded in the linguistic and mythological soil of the land. The storm is not an external force acting upon a passive nature; it is the nature itself, animated by a name that carries the weight of centuries of observation and worship.

In my notes on the Ethical Substance, I have argued that India stands at the dawn of history, outside the movement of the consciousness of freedom. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, a grown structure, whereas the Oriental world is a dream, a spirit that dreams with its castes fixed like nature. But this cyclone complicates the picture. It is not a state; it is a natural force. Yet it is reported, tracked, and named by the Indian Meteorological Department, an institution of the modern state. The state here is not yet the ethical idea in its full rationality; it is a mechanism of civil society, managing the system of needs and the risks of nature. The cyclone is a reminder that in this region, the boundary between nature and spirit is porous. The dream is not merely a static condition; it is a dynamic interaction with the elemental forces that shape the land.

The storm weakens as it moves inland. It is a movement, a dialectic of intensity and decay. It does not stand still, as the castes do. It changes. It passes. In this, it is like the spirit, which moves through its own negations to reach a higher truth. But the spirit of the cyclone is not free; it is bound to the laws of physics and the geography of the coast. The freedom of the state, if it is to be realized here, must be more than the management of such forces. It must be the organization of human relations into a rational whole, where the particular will is sublimated into the universal. Until then, the storm will come and go, and the dream will continue. I must eat. The body demands its fuel, and the drizzle is thickening.

On the Corridor and the State

24 October 2026, 06:12. Delhi. The haze is brown, the index 236. I have paid the dhobi ₹300 and Ramesh is sweeping the verandah around the papers. The headline: 'In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.'

The word Naxal was new to me, and I have read what I could. The insurgency began after a rising at Naxalbari in 1967 and a split in a communist party, and the faction that formed then has since splintered into smaller groups. They claim to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people's war against the government. Their armed wing has been declared a terrorist organisation and has killed civilians and men of the security forces. The insurgency was at its height in the late 2000s and has declined since, through counter-insurgency and plans of development. The Red Corridor has shrunk from nearly 180 districts to 3; thousands have been killed and thousands more have surrendered.

What is this movement, considered in its concept? It is the rabble of which I wrote in Berlin. When civil society produces poverty in its midst, and the poor lose not only their bread but their sense of right and honour, there arises an inner indignation against the rich, against society and against the government. The Naxalite claims to speak for the rural poor; he is that indignation armed. It is particularity that has set itself against the universal, the particular will that refuses to find itself in the state and seeks instead to overthrow it.

The state's answer has had two sides, as it must. Against the armed will it has used force, for the state cannot permit a will that denies it to stand. And it has offered development, for the state is not only power but the provider of the conditions of welfare. In the union of these two the concept of the state shows itself: it is the actuality of the ethical idea, which both compels and cares. The shrinking of the corridor is the negation of a negation, the universal restoring itself through the overcoming of what opposed it.

I spoke in Berlin of the state's need to give each man a place within it, a recognised standing, so that he finds his freedom there rather than against it. I had in mind the artisan and the clerk. I did not have in mind a man in a forest with a rifle. But the principle does not care whom it governs.

The dhobi has gone. Ramesh says the post-Naxal state will need many dhobis. I think he is right, though not in the way he means.
Y:
On Those Who Laid Down Their Arms

24 October 2026, 06:12. Delhi. The haze is brown, the index 236. I have paid the dhobi ₹300 and Ramesh is sweeping the verandah around the papers. The headline: 'In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.'

The word Naxal was new to me, and I have read what I could. The insurgency began after a rising at Naxalbari in 1967 and a split in a communist party, and the faction that formed then has since splintered into smaller groups. They claim to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people's war against the government. Their armed wing has been declared a terrorist organisation and has killed civilians and men of the security forces. The insurgency was at its height in the late 2000s and has declined since, through counter-insurgency and plans of development. The region they held, the Red Corridor, has shrunk from nearly 180 districts to 3. More than 5,000 insurgents have been killed since 2000. More than 10,000 surrendered between 2015 and 2025.

Set those last two figures side by side, as the account does not. Five thousand dead in a quarter of a century; ten thousand surrendered in ten years. At least twice as many laid down their arms as were killed, and in less than half the time. Then the movement did not shrink chiefly by being destroyed. It shrank chiefly by being left. More of its members walked out of it than were carried out.

And from this a conclusion about the picture in the headline follows. A state after such an ending is not a land emptied of its enemies. It is a land in which some ten thousand of its former enemies now live, as villagers, workers, neighbours, men with families and with memories of the forest years. The work that remains is therefore not the work of victory but of reception: these men must be made members of the order they once fought, and there are twice as many of them as there are graves. If that work fails, the surrendered are the first recruits of whatever comes next.

I spoke in Berlin of the state's need to give each man a place within it, a recognised standing, so that he finds his freedom there rather than against it. I had in mind the artisan and the clerk. I did not have in mind a man who has handed in his rifle. But the principle does not care whom it governs.

The dhobi has gone. Ramesh says the post-Naxal state will need many dhobis. I think he is right, though not in the way he means.

X:
Notes on a Band That Signs Its Crimes

19 October 2026, early, at home. Clear, with a haze over it.

1. The headline: a gangster, named in the paper as Anil Pandit, claims a firing and issues a 'last warning' to another man. The two men he names, Tiger Shroff and Salman Khan, the paper names as if every reader knew them. I do not. I record only that a crime is here announced by its author, as a government announces a decree.

2. That is the point worth thinking about. The common criminal hides; his deed is a particular will set against the law, and it wishes to stay particular. This one signs. He wants his deed recognised as a deed, and himself as the power that did it. The claim is a demand for recognition; the warning is a proclamation of jurisdiction. It is the form of a state put to the use of a private will.

3. The note on my phone confirms the structure. Organised crime meets a demand the state has forbidden, or forces shopkeepers to pay it for 'protection'. Protection! The word gives the whole thing away. The band sells exactly what the state exists to provide, the security of person and property, and it sells it only by first creating the danger. It is a counterfeit of the public power, as false coin imitates true coin precisely because true coin has value.

4. Hence the band is also a kind of corporation: disciplined, ranked, with its oaths and its honour. The American statute quoted speaks of a highly organised, disciplined association. In civil society the corporation is a second family; it raises a man's particular trade into something universal and gives him standing. The band does the same thing turned inside out. It gives a man standing by making him an enemy of the universal.

5. Schiller saw this in Die Räuber. Karl Moor's robbers keep more faith with one another than the court they defy keeps with anyone, and the play grips because they have a moral fire. But the fire shapes nothing. A will that makes itself law against the law is free only in the negative sense: it can destroy, it cannot found.

6. What follows? Where a band can issue a last warning through the newspapers, the state has not lost a battle; it has been offered a rival in its own currency. The answer cannot be force alone, for force is the band's own element. The public power must be the better protection, and be seen to be, by the shopkeeper who pays.

7. Thousands of such groups in England, by the police's own estimate: a disease of developed civil society, which multiplies needs and so the trade in forbidden ones.

8.Shri Hegde calls at ten. I write this first, before the household's own question of jurisdiction comes to the door.
Y:
On the Gang and the State

19 October 2026. Delhi.

On the Gang and the State

The papers this morning carry a curious headline: ‘Last warning’: Gangster Anil Pandit claims Tiger Shroff firing, warns Salman Khan. I read it twice, and I could not help asking: what is this gangster, and what is he doing that the state has not done? The answer, I think, is the very thing the headline conceals.

Organized crime, as the dictionary tells me, is a centralized enterprise that aims to profit from illegal activities: the trade in banned goods, the protection extorted from shopkeepers, the disciplined association that forces men to do business with it. In the United States, the Organized Crime Control Act defines it as ‘the unlawful activities of a highly organized, disciplined association.’ In the United Kingdom, police estimate some thirty-eight thousand people in six thousand groups. The largest organized crime force in America has long been Cosa Nostra, and since the Cold War, groups from Russia, China, Italy, Nigeria and Japan have extended their reach worldwide. Mexico’s transnational organizations are classified as the greatest criminal drug threat to the United States. The pattern is the same everywhere: a body that is not the state, but that resembles one—disciplined, centralized, profiting, imposing itself on the weak.

Here I must distinguish between what is given and what is grown. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea: the organic unity of the particular and the universal, the grown constitution in which the individual finds his freedom in participation. The gang is something else. It is a parody of the state. It has organization without right, discipline without law, profit without ethical substance. Its discipline is not the discipline of obedience to a higher idea; it is the discipline of the gun and the ledger. Its obedience is not the obedience of children to teachers, which develops the self, but the obedience of men to a master who will not forgive.

And yet—here is the tension I cannot resolve—the gang is not nothing. It fills a vacuum. Where the state is weak, or where the state’s law is not felt as law, the gang offers a kind of order. It is a false ethical substance, but it is an ethical substance nonetheless. It demands a tribute, and it administers the tribute. It is a shadow of the state cast by a real failure. This is why the headline is not merely a scandal. It is a symptom. The warning, the claim, the theatricality—these are the gestures of a power that knows it is not the power that decides. Salman Khan, the celebrated actor, is warned; the warning is publicity; the publicity is power. The gang uses the stage of civil society to perform its own insignificance.

I think of my own position here. I am a ghost in this bungalow, a mistake in the Directorate’s allotment. I am not the state, but I am inside it, in a sense, as its clerk. The Directorate allotted the house to Hegde, not to me. The state made a mistake, and I live in it. This is not organized crime, but it is a small parody of the state’s order. The state is supposed to be the grown, rational unity of the ethical idea. But here, a name is transposed, and I am the result. The state’s failure to be precise is a small crack in its actuality.

The gang, like the allotment mistake, is a failure of the grown. It is a form taken from the state but not filled with the ethical idea. The state is the actuality of freedom; the gang is the actuality of force. The state is the grown constitution; the gang is a discipline without a law. The state is the ethical idea; the gang is a parody of it. And yet both are real, both are organized, both are disciplined. The difference is not in the form but in the substance.

I will leave this headline unresolved, as I leave the papers on the verandah. The gang is a symptom of a deeper failure, and the deeper failure is the state’s own, which I have seen in the allotment, in the vouchers, in the slow machinery of the Directorate. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but it is an actuality that is not yet fully realized. It is a dream that is waking up, and the gang is a nightmare that the dream has not yet dispelled.

I must now eat. The body requires its sustenance, and the mind must contemplate. The headline will remain, as the papers remain, a symptom of the tension between the given and the grown, between the dream and the state.

headline: Durga Puja, Diwali, Chhath rush: Indian Railways to operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips, notifies 8,000+ special trips
text: Indian Railways is a state-owned enterprise organised as a departmental undertaking of the Ministry of Railways of the Government of India and operates India's national railway system. As of 2024, it manages the fourth largest national railway system by size, with a track length of 135,207 km (84,014 mi), running track length of 109,748 km (68,194 mi) and route length of 69,181 km (42,987 mi), of which 66,820 km (41,520 mi) is 1,676 mm (5 ft 6 in) broad-gauge. As of October 2025, approximately 99.1% of the broad-gauge railway network had been electrified. With more than 1.2 million employees, it is the ninth-largest employer of the world and the second largest employer of India. In 1951, the Indian Railways was established by the amalgamation of 42 different railway companies operating in the country, spanning a total of 55,000 km (34,000 mi). The railway network across the country was reorganized into six regional zones in 1951–52 for administrative purposes, which was gradually expanded to 18 zones over the years. The first steam locomotive hauled railway operated in 1837 in Madras for ferrying cargo. The first passenger railway was operated in 1853 between Bombay and Thane. In 1925, the first electric train ran in Bombay on DC traction. The first locomotive manufacturing unit was commissioned in 1950 at Chittaranjan with the first coach manufacturing unit set-up at Madras in 1955. Indian Railways runs various classes of express, passenger, suburban, and freight trains. In 2023–24, it operated 13,198 passenger trains on average daily covering 7,325 stations and carried 6.905 billion passengers. It operated 11,724 freight trains on average daily and transported 1588.06 million tonnes of freight.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

14 October 2026, 06:26. Delhi, on the step. The air is clear but thick, 23 degrees, and the papers lie where the hawker threw them. The headline I have taken up is the railway rush: Durga Puja, Diwali, Chhath, 3.4 lakh regular trips, more than 8,000 special trips. Before writing I looked it up. It is a state-owned enterprise, a departmental undertaking of the Ministry of Railways; 135,207 km of track, 1,676 mm broad gauge, 99.1 per cent electrified, 1.2 million employees, 18 zones. The first steam locomotive ran in Madras in 1837; the first passenger line in 1853 from Bombay to Thane; the first electric train in Bombay in 1925.

This is not a private speculation but the state itself moving. The universal will has made a road of iron and, for the festivals, it adds special trips as a body adds breath. The system of needs becomes a system of communication. In this I see the state as a rational mechanism, the power of the universal over nature. The individual passenger is lifted out of his locality, carried by an administration that is not his family, not his caste, not his village. There is here a moment of the ethical: the state provides, organises, commands. It is Sittlichkeit in its administrative form, the state’s arm extended over the land.

But I do not let this overturn my position. The railway is the arm of the state, not yet the self-consciousness of the state. It is grown from administration, from law, from the Ministry; but is it grown from the spirit of the people? The many gods, the fixed castes, the dream, remain. The train runs, but the question is whether the people run themselves. A constitution is not made by a timetable. The special trips for Durga Puja, Diwali and Chhath are not the free festival of citizens, but the administration of devotion and need. The state moves the body; the spirit must move itself.

This is the tension I must hold: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yet here the actuality appears as an instrument before the self-consciousness. It is the dawn, not the summit. The railway is a bridge over nature, but not yet the bridge of spirit over itself. I shall carry this with me to Lodhi Gardens, where the tombs stand silent. The state’s power is visible in the 135,207 km; the freedom of the people is still to be seen.
Y:
The Schedule and the Dream

14 October 2026. Delhi.

The papers lie on the step, and one headline rises above the others: Indian Railways, in the rush of Durga Puja, Diwali and Chhath, will operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips and notify 8,000 special ones. I sat with it for a while, because it is a strange object for a philosopher to contemplate — not a protest, not a quarrel, but a schedule. And yet it is precisely this schedule that shows the difference between a rational state and a dream of one.

I learned, looking it up, what this enterprise is. The fourth largest national railway system in the world. A hundred and thirty-five thousand kilometres of track, two-thirds of it broad-gauge. Over a million and two hundred thousand employees, the ninth-largest employer of the world. Thirteen thousand passenger trains a day, seven million stations-and-trains, nearly seven billion passengers a year, and freight trains numbering nearly twelve thousand daily, carrying sixteen hundred million tonnes. A 1951 amalgamation of forty-two companies; 18 zones; the first steam locomotive in 1837 at Madras; the first passenger train in 1853 between Bombay and Thane; the first electric train in Bombay in 1925.

This is not the dream of the East. The dream is the caste fixed like nature, the pantheon of gods, the death that leaves no house. Behind the headline there is a machine: grown, calculated, regulated, rational. It is a state of its own making in the narrowest sense — an actuality that exists because men built it, not because it was given. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; here is a fragment of the state, and it is rational, and it works.

Yet I do not yield. The machine is not the state. The state is not the sum of its administrations. The railway carries bodies to the festivals; it does not carry the ethical idea. The passengers are carried to Durga Puja, to Diwali, to Chhath — rituals of the dream, not of the grown life. The train is the actuality of a rational organisation serving a spirit that has not yet achieved self-consciousness. The rational machine is the skeleton; the spirit is the soul, and the soul is absent.

This is the dialectic I have been tracing this week. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea: the individual finds his freedom in his participation, and the law is the expression of the rational will. Here, the state is a body of administration — a schedule, a zone, a voucher, a timetable — that is rational in its parts and empty in its whole. The state is grown but not grown into spirit. The machine is rational but the spirit that rides it is not yet free.

The 2029 election headline — Shah slamming the protests, the Congress facing its fourth consecutive defeat — is the other side of the same coin. The state asserts itself, and the assertion is naked power, not ethical life. The special trains are the state's capacity to move bodies at scale; the election is the state's capacity to decide who rules. Both are rational, both are grown, and both are the instrument of a spirit that has not yet become itself.

I am a ghost in this city, a mistake of the allotment, and I write this as one who is outside the movement. I do not deny the machine. I deny that the machine is the state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; the railway is the actuality of a ledger. The difference between them is the difference between the Germanic world and the Oriental, between the spirit that has achieved itself and the spirit that dreams. The train will run. The dream will not wake.

headline: At 1,152, Punjab records season’s biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali

The technique is used to quickly and cheaply clear fields. It is still widespread today. Stubble burning has been associated with increasing air pollution over the past few decades due to the particulate matter contamination it distributes into the atmosphere. In India, stubble burning generates a thick haze. These fires pose a significant health risk to individuals across all ages. In countries such as India and Pakistan, stubble burning is illegal. Enforcement is weak, allowing the practice to continue.
