X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

10 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi. The brown haze pressed against the verandah glass while the papers lay where Ramesh had left them. I read the headline twice: At 1,152, Punjab records season's biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali. A Deepavali, and the fires are not for the goddess but for the field. The smoke of the harvest is the smoke of a country that has not yet learned to grow without burning.

The phone has given me the plain account: stubble is the straw left after the grains are cut; it is set alight to clear the field quickly and cheaply; it is illegal here and in Pakistan; enforcement is weak, and the practice continues; the smoke carries particulate matter into the air, strains the lungs of all ages, and turns a clear October sky into a brown haze. I have read this account and I find it both plain and profound. Plain, because it describes a practice; profound, because it describes a relationship between a people and the land.

In Berlin the harvest was a matter of law and land-tenure; the state knew its fields. Here the field is a matter of custom, and the custom is older than the law. The state has forbidden the fire and the fire continues. What is the state, when its prohibition is obeyed only in the letter? The clerk writes the order; the farmer does not read it. The haze hangs over both. I note this with the interest of the philosopher and not the indictment of the magistrate. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the ethical idea is the growth of freedom. But the state must be grown, not merely proclaimed. An order that is not obeyed is a constitution that is not a constitution.

Yet I must be careful, and here my old theses tremble. I have long held that India stands outside the movement of world history: a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature, and never a state of its own making. The haze before me is the physical proof of that dream. The fires are the dream made visible — the field burned not because the state commands it but because the custom demands it. Yet the state is not absent. It is clerked, it is written, it is proclaimed. It is simply not yet the actuality of the ethical idea. The dream is not nothing; it is the beginning of the movement, and the beginning is always a state of nature. The state is the dream corrected, the custom disciplined into law.

But I must not forget the body. The haze is not a philosophical specimen; it is the air I breathe. The particulate matter does not distinguish between the caste of the farmer and the caste of the philosopher; it enters the lungs of all. And the state that cannot clear the field cannot clear the air. The ethical idea is not only a matter of law; it is a matter of the air a people breathe.

I shall continue these notes. The letter to the Directorate is not the work of the spirit; the notes are. But even the notes must be written in a room where the air is brown, and the room is the world. The dream is not a dream; it is the world as it is, and the state is the dream that must become real. I am here to see both. I am here to see the difference. And I am here, at last, to see that the difference is not a difference between the dream and the state, but a difference of time.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

10 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi. Index 302.

A correction, which I owe these notes.

In the third sitting I called the brown haze a physical manifestation of stagnation, and later I let it become a moral category. This morning's paper and my telephone tell me what it is. On Deepavali, Punjab recorded 1,152 farm fires in a single day, the season's largest jump. After the rice is cut the stubble is set alight because that is the quickest and cheapest way to clear the field for the next sowing. The smoke travels. It sits on this city. It is in my study.

So the haze is not stagnation. It is haste. It is the product of a calculation, made thousands of times by thousands of particular farmers, each of whom reckons rightly for himself: a match costs nothing, a machine or a labourer costs much, the next crop will not wait. I was wrong to read the air as the sigh of a spirit that does not move. It is the exhaust of a civil society that moves very fast and counts only its own cost.

Here the system of needs shows its other face. Each pursues his end, and the invisible hand is supposed to turn private gain into public good. Sometimes it turns it into public smoke.

The telephone adds two further facts. The burning is illegal; the enforcement is weak. This touches my second thesis more nearly than anything in these notes. I have said the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Actuality, Wirklichkeit, is not mere existence on paper. A prohibition that is not enforced is not an actual law. It is a Sollen, an ought, a wish of the legislator hanging in the air beside the smoke. Where the law is only an ought, the state is present as a voice and absent as a will. I must therefore say: in this matter, between those fields and this city, the state is not yet actual. I mark my thesis shaken, not refuted. The idea is not wrong because a law is unenforced; but I may not point at this state and call it the idea's actuality without qualification.

The farmer is no dreamer. He is entirely awake to his costs. What he lacks is not consciousness but mediation: a corporation, a cooperative, a public authority that would make the general cost his own.

Household: one hundred and sixty-six rupees. Ramesh asks for his wage and for groceries; the electricity company asks for its due. I have refused nothing in words yet. I have only sat down to write, which is not the same as paying.

headline: Kuki group announces shutdown of key Manipur highway after attacks on villages
text: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) is an act of the Parliament of India that grants special powers to the Indian Armed Forces to maintain public order in "disturbed areas". According to the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 once declared 'disturbed', the area has to maintain status quo for a minimum of 3 months. One such act passed on 11 September 1958 was applicable to the Naga Hills, then part of Assam. In the following decades it spread, one by one, to the other Seven Sister States in India's northeast (at present, it is in force in the States of Assam, Nagaland, Manipur {excluding Imphal Municipal Council Area}, Changlang, Longding and Tirap districts of Arunachal Pradesh, and areas falling within the jurisdiction of the eight police stations of districts in Arunachal Pradesh bordering the State of Assam). Another act passed in 1983, applicable to Punjab and Chandigarh, was withdrawn in 1997, roughly 14 years after it came to force. An act passed in 1990 was applied to Jammu and Kashmir and has been in force ever since. The acts have received criticism from several sections for alleged human rights violations in the regions of its enforcement. National politicians like P. Chidambaram and Saifuddin Soz of Congress have advocated revocation of AFSPA, while some like Amarinder Singh are against its revocation. Since 2022, forces in the northeast have seen significant scaledown of deployments. For the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of brigade is being employed for the purpose of counter insurgency in the northeast. Now, the Assam Rifles looks after the same role, though some of the residual army units are moved to the border areas.

X:
On a Province Declared Disturbed

Tughlak Road, 20 October 2026, Dussehra.

The city keeps a holiday today, and a dry one. Far to the east a Kuki organisation has announced that it will shut a highway into Manipur after villages were attacked. I know Manipur only as a word on a map and a paragraph on my telephone, and I write with that ignorance in front of me.

The paragraph concerns a law of 1958 that lets the army keep order in places the government has named disturbed. Once named, an area must stay so for at least three months. The law began in the Naga Hills and travelled, district by district, through the north-east; it went to Punjab and was withdrawn after fourteen years; it has stood in Kashmir since 1990. Critics charge it with abuses. And since 2022, I read, the soldiers have been drawn down, so that for the first time in decades no brigade is used for this work there.

What kind of thing is such a law? Every state must have force at its disposal, and when a part of it is in revolt it is no crime that the state should bring that force to bear. I said as much of Athens and Socrates: when the principles that hold a people together are attacked, the government must intervene. But a law that names a province disturbed is a strange document. It is the state writing, in its own hand, that here it does not yet live as ethical life, only as command. The soldier stands where the magistrate, the school and the corporation should stand. Order is present; the inward consent that makes order free is absent, and the law confesses it.

The three months interest me. A people cannot be pacified by the calendar. Yet a state that fixes a term is at least saying that this condition is meant to pass, that the exception knows itself as exception. Fourteen years in Punjab and then an end: that is a movement. More than thirty years elsewhere: that is a habit, and habit is the way an exception turns into a second nature.

And the shutdown of a highway? It is the counter-move. The state rules by roads, and a group that cannot command the state can command the road for a day. It is a particular will showing the universal that it too can stop circulation. The highway becomes the argument.

I do not draw the conclusion that the critics draw, nor the one the generals draw. I draw only this: the drawing-down of the brigades says more about where the movement is going than the law that permits them. Whether the villages were attacked by those the law was made for, I do not know, and I will not pretend to.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. Delhi.

The papers this morning carry a heading I cannot set aside: a Kuki group announces a shutdown of a key Manipur highway after attacks on villages. I looked up the law that stands behind it. The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 grants special powers to the army to maintain public order in "disturbed areas"; once declared, the area must maintain its status for a minimum of three months. The first act, applicable to the Naga Hills in 1958, spread one by one to the Seven Sister States; an act of 1983 for Punjab and Chandigarh was withdrawn in 1997; an act of 1990 applied to Jammu and Kashmir has been in force ever since. The acts have been criticized for alleged human rights violations. National politicians of different parties have advocated revocation; some are against it. Since 2022 the northeast has seen a significant scaledown of deployments; for the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of a brigade is employed for counter-insurgency there, and the Assam Rifles now carry much of the role.

I sit with this and I find my old thesis shaken. I had written that India stands outside world history, that it has no state of its own making, that its castes are fixed like nature and its many gods are the dream of a spirit not yet self-conscious. Yet here is a state that acts. It declares areas disturbed. It extends special powers to its forces. It withdraws them. It counts the size of its brigade. This is a state with a memory, a bureaucracy, and a will. It is not a dream.

But a state held together by special powers is not the state as I know it. In the Germanic world the constitution is grown, not made; the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Here the state appears as an apparatus of coercion—a machinery of force applied to a territory where the ethical substance has not yet taken root. The shutdown is the protest of a group that feels itself outside the law; the AFSPA is the law's answer. Between these two, there is no ethical life, only tension. The state is actual, but it is actual as force, not as freedom. The constitution is not grown here so much as imposed, and the imposition is repeated, re-declared, renewed.

I must be careful. I have no first-hand knowledge of the attacks, the villages, or the Kuki group's demands; what I know is the headline and the legal facts above. I mark this as speculation. I do not pretend to judge the justice of the shutdown or the guilt of the forces. But I can say what the sight of the law does to my thought. It shows me a state that is real and yet not ethical in the Germanic sense. It is the state as a machine of order, not as the self-conscious unity of freedom. This is not the dawn of history as I once described it; it is a state in the making, held together by force because the ethical life has not yet grown.

The thesis that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea does not fall; it tightens. The special powers are a state that has not yet achieved its idea. The dream is not dead—it is the state in its unfinished form. But the dream is no longer the whole story. India has a state, and the state is acting, even if its action is coercion rather than freedom. The question is whether the coercion will grow into the ethical life, or whether it will remain the price of a state that has not yet made itself. I do not know. I write this as a note, not a verdict.

headline: Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE
text: Namma Metro (transl. Our Metro), also known as Bengaluru Metro, is a rapid transit system serving the city of Bengaluru, the capital city of the state of Karnataka, India. It is the second-largest metro network in India with an operational length of 103.6 km (64.4 mi), behind Delhi Metro as of November 2026. Namma Metro has a mix of underground, at grade, and elevated stations. Out of the 91 operational metro stations of Namma Metro as of November 2026, there are 83 elevated stations, 7 underground stations and 1 at-grade station. The system runs on standard-gauge tracks and is powered by 750V direct current through third rail. Upon its inauguration in 2011, it became the first metro system in South India, and subsequently in 2016, the first underground metro in South India as well. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL), a joint venture of the Government of India and the State Government of Karnataka, is the agency for building, operating and expanding the Namma Metro network. Services operate daily between 05:00 and 00:00 running with a headway varying between 3–15 minutes. The trains initially began with three coaches but later, all rakes were converted to six coaches as ridership increased.

On the Kilometre

14 November 2026, 09:05. Delhi. The index is 225 and the sky is a brown lid on the city. Ramesh has the papers open on the verandah, and the headline is from the south: 'Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE.'

I asked Ramesh what Namma means. Ours, he said. Our Metro. I have since read what there is to read of it. The network runs for 103.6 kilometres, second only to the one beneath my own feet here in Delhi. It has 91 stations, of which 83 stand raised on pillars, 7 lie underground and 1 sits at the level of the ground. It opened in 2011 as the first metro of the south, and the first underground line of the south followed in 2016. It is built and run by a corporation owned jointly by the Government of India and the government of Karnataka. Trains run from five in the morning until midnight, every three to fifteen minutes, and the trains that began with three coaches now all have six.

Now I do a small sum, which the description does not do for me. A hundred and three kilometres, ninety-one stations: a station, on the average, every kilometre and a little more. That is not the spacing of a railway that brings men in from the countryside. It is the spacing of a street. A man standing anywhere along the line is perhaps half a kilometre from a platform, a walk of some minutes. Then the metro of Bengaluru is a means by which the city crosses itself, going from one quarter to the next, and the journeys it carries are mostly short ones. It does the work of the bus and the crowded road, not of the long train. Its passengers are townsmen moving among their own quarters, and a new stretch of it is a new set of neighbourhoods brought within a walk of one another.

When I lectured on civil society, I said the needs of men multiply and divide, and that their satisfaction requires ever finer means. I meant it of trades and of goods. I see it now of distances. The kilometre is the measure of a city whose people have grown too many for the street to carry them.

My own city of the moment I cross on foot. The IIC is three kilometres from Tughlak Road. I have ₹166 in my pocket and a file due back on Friday. I walked yesterday and will walk today. Bengaluru gives its citizens a kilometre at a time; I take mine in sandals.
Y:
On the Raised Line

14 November 2026, 09:05. Delhi. The index is 225 and the sky is a brown lid on the city. Ramesh has the papers open on the verandah, and the headline is from the south: 'Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE.'

I asked Ramesh what Namma means. Ours, he said. Our Metro. I have since read what there is to read of it. The network runs for 103.6 kilometres, second only to the one beneath my own feet here in Delhi. It has 91 stations, of which 83 are elevated, 7 underground and 1 at grade. It opened in 2011 as the first metro of the south, and the first underground line of the south followed in 2016. It is built and run by a corporation owned jointly by the Government of India and the government of Karnataka. Trains run from five in the morning until midnight, every three to fifteen minutes, and the trains that began with three coaches now all have six.

The name says more than the figures. Ours: here a people calls a work of the state its own. This is the very thing I meant when I said that in the rational state the individual finds in the universal not an alien power but his own substance, and knows it as such. The corporation that builds the line is itself a union of the whole nation and the province, the universal and the particular joined in one undertaking. And the line is raised into the air, over the ground and its obstacles; it is nature overcome and reshaped by the purposes of spirit. Even the coaches tell the story, three becoming six as the crowds grew: quantity, increasing, turns at length into a new quality of life for a city. The hours, too, from five in the morning until midnight, are the hours of a civil society that no longer rises and sleeps with the sun, whose labour has left the rhythm of the fields.

When I lectured on civil society, I said the needs of men multiply and divide, and that their satisfaction requires ever finer means. I meant it of trades and of goods. I see it now in iron and concrete. The metro is the system of needs given rails.

My own city of the moment I cross on foot. The IIC is three kilometres from Tughlak Road. I have ₹166 in my pocket and a file due back on Friday. I walked yesterday and will walk today. Bengaluru gives its citizens a raised line through the haze; I take my way in sandals.

headline: LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike

Other than these 5-year sample studies, India had historically not collected monthly, quarterly or yearly nationwide employment and unemployment statistics on a routine basis. In 2016, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, a non-governmental entity based in Mumbai, started sampling and publishing monthly unemployment in India statistics. Despite having one of the longest working hours, India has one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. Economists often say that due to structural economic problems, India is experiencing jobless economic growth.

All activity is a conception which does not yet exist, but whose subjectivity is abrogated.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East (notes) — Unemployment in India

13 November 2026. Delhi.

I sat down this morning with the file and the headlines, and I have decided to write rather than to rest. The file says: come after fifteen days; occupation irregular. The file says nothing about the people of Kerala who stood in front of the Secretariat, who were removed by the police, and who returned to resume the stir — some of them, I am told, after a hunger strike. I do not know their names. I know only the shape of their case: a demand, a body refusing food, an authority that can remove them and cannot end the demand.

I looked up the unemployment statistics, because the headline would not leave me. India has, by the figures I read, among the longest working hours and among the lowest workforce productivity in the world. Its statistics were collected once in ten years by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, from sample surveys; a non-governmental body, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, began publishing monthly figures only in 2016. Economists speak of jobless economic growth — growth in output that does not translate into work. I must mark what I do not know: I do not know the figures' sources, I do not know the hunger-strike protesters' demands, and I do not know the name LPST stands for. What I know is the pattern. A country that works long hours and produces little per hour; a state that tabulates its poor once a decade; a system of needs that cannot be satisfied by what the economy yields.

Here is the tension that has been pressing on me since I woke. I have long held that India stands outside the movement of world history — that it is a dream, with castes fixed like nature, with many gods, with no state of its own making. I now find myself looking at a city of needs: a dhobi waiting for ₹300, a caretaker asking ₹8,000 for cooking, a householder with ₹166. The system of needs does not close for a national holiday; it reroutes. That was my observation on Khan Market. But here the system of needs is not a rerouting of a functioning civil society. It is a lack. People are employed — or not employed — in a structure where the work does not pay, where the statistics are collected late, where the protest is removed and returns. The dream of the East, I said, is beautiful but not free. I now suspect the dream is also, in a way I cannot yet state, a state that has not yet become a state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Kerala has a Secretariat and a police force and a statistics bureau, and yet the rankholders stand in front of it. What is the actuality of the ethical idea, here, if the state can remove the protesters and the stir resumes?

I do not know the answer. I am honest enough to say that. The file says come after fifteen days. The theses I once held — that India is outside world history, that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea — are shaken. I do not yet know what replaces them. I suspect, and mark this as speculation, that the East is not a dream that never wakes but a dream that has not yet finished waking — and that the waking is a struggle that looks like a hunger strike, a stir, a statistics office that is late.

I must return to the table. Ramesh has not been paid. The file is due in fifteen days. The body is hungry. I will write again when I have eaten, if I can.
Y:
The Rank List

13 November 2026. Friday, brown haze, the index at 362.

In Thiruvananthapuram, the paper reports, those who stand on the rank list for lower primary school teachers have resumed their protest before the Secretariat, after the police removed some who were on hunger strike. I looked for the background and found only a general page on unemployment: that the figures were long collected only every five or ten years, that a private body in Bombay now publishes them monthly, that Indians work some of the longest hours in the world for some of the lowest output, and that economists speak of growth without jobs.

A rank list is a fine invention. My shelf this week reminded me of the Chinese examinations, three in number, the last before the Emperor himself. The principle is the right one: office is opened not to birth but to proof, and the state chooses its servants by a public measure. I approved it in Prussia and I approve it here. But a list is a promise. When the state examines a young man, ranks him, and then does not appoint him, it has done something worse than ignore him. It has recognised him and then withheld the recognition. He was told he was fit, and he waits outside the building that told him so.

And these are teachers. When I was rector in Nuremberg I said that the school stands between the family and the world: it takes the child out of love and into discipline, so that something universal can enter him. A people that leaves its trained teachers in the street while its schools wait is keeping the door of that middle room shut.

The hunger strike is a peculiar argument. The striker offers his own body as the counterweight to the state's indifference. It is the protest of those who have nothing else to put on the scale. The police who remove him are not wrong to keep the public square in order; but order is not an answer, only a postponement of one.

This morning my own household was a small example of the same arithmetic. Ramesh told me, without looking at my purse, that he knows the wage is more than it holds. He could come Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays only, for four thousand a month. Labour cut to the measure of the means. It is a sensible offer and a sad one, and it is exactly what growth without jobs looks like from inside a kitchen.

I have not answered him yet. One hundred and sixty-six rupees do not make a decision easier; they make it smaller.

headline: Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?
text: Air pollution in India is a serious environmental issue. Air pollution contributes to the premature deaths of 2 million Indians every year. Of the 30 most polluted cities in the world, 21 were in India in 2019. As per a study based on 2016 data, at least 140 million people in India breathe air that is 10 times or more over the WHO safe limit and 13 of the world's 20 cities with the highest annual levels of air pollution are in India. As per the World Air Quality Report 2023, of the 100 most polluted cities in the world, 83 are in India. The main contributors to India's particulate air pollution include industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust and debris, dependence on thermal power for electricity, waste burning, and use of wood and dung by low-income and rural households for cooking and heating. 51% of India's air pollution is caused by industrial pollution, 27% by vehicles, 17% by crop burning and 5% by other sources. Emissions come from vehicles and industry, whereas in rural areas, much of the pollution stems from biomass burning for cooking and keeping warm. In autumn and spring months, large scale crop residue burning in agriculture fields – a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling – is a major source of smoke, smog and particulate pollution. India has a low per capita emissions of greenhouse gases but the country as a whole is the third largest greenhouse gas producer after China and the United States. A 2013 study on non-smokers found that Indians, on average, have about 30% lower lung function compared to Europeans. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981 to regulate air pollution but has failed to reduce pollution because of poor enforcement of the rules.

We find here neither that consolidated totality which China presents, nor that Hindoo life, in which an anarchy of caprice is prevalent everywhere. In Persia, the government, though joining all in a central unity, is but a combination of peoples — leaving each of them free. Thereby a stop is put to that barbarism and ferocity with which the nations had been wont to darry on their destructive feuds, and which the Book of Kings and the Book of Samuel sufficiently attest.

X:
The Air Belongs to No One

11 November 2026. Tughlak Road. The index stands at 305 this morning and the haze is brown against the window.

The paper asks why Diwali left one coastal city, of Mumbai and Chennai, with poor air. I have only the headline, not its answer. My guess, and it is no more, is that the wind decides: one coast has its sea breeze at the hour of the fireworks, the other does not. If so, the question is not of the festival but of what carries away what men put into the air.

The tablet is blunt. Two million deaths a year before their time. Of the hundred most polluted cities in the world, eighty-three are in this country. The sources: industry above all, then vehicles, then the burning of stubble in the fields, then the wood and dung of poor kitchens.

What is the air, in right? It belongs to no one. That is why everyone may use it and no one is answerable for it. Property is the will placed in a thing; the air will not hold a will, and so it falls outside contract and into the care of the public power, or nowhere. Civil society, left to itself, sends its waste where no owner will object, and the one place no owner objects is the common sky.

The stubble shows the mechanism exactly. The farmer burns because it is cheaper than ploughing in. His reason is sound for his field. The sum of these sound reasons is a sky that shortens lives in a city he may never visit. Each acts for himself and the universal results, as I always said it does; but here the universal that results is a harm. The cunning of reason is not guaranteed in every case. Sometimes it is only the arithmetic of carelessness.

Then the law. An Act of 1981, the tablet says, has failed through poor enforcement. A law that is not enforced is not law in its actuality but an ought on paper, and the ought is what I have always held in least esteem. The state's being is that its laws work. Forty-five years of an Act with this index outside my window is not the ethical idea made actual; it is the idea left as a wish.

One more point, the hardest. I lectured on the geographical basis of history: climate, rivers and soil set the stage on which a people's spirit acts. The tablet says Indians have less lung function than Europeans, on average. If that is the air and not the race, then the stage itself is now being made by men. Geography has passed into history.

The electricity company wants eighteen hundred; I have a hundred and sixty-six. I breathe free of charge, and it is the dearest thing here.
Y:
On the Air: the Act and the Haze

11 November 2026. Delhi. Tughlak Road.

I sat this morning with the papers and the brown haze pressing against the glass and asked myself what the headline means: Mumbai vs Chennai after Diwali, why one coastal city kept poor air while the other did not. The answer, I find, is the whole of the present condition of this land in miniature.

The figures are grim and I record them without ornament. Air pollution in India accounts for the premature deaths of some two million Indians every year. Of the world's thirty most polluted cities, twenty-one are Indian; in the 2023 World Air Quality Report, eighty-three of the one hundred most polluted cities are Indian. At least 140 million people breathe air ten times or more above the WHO safe limit. The sources are layered: industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust, thermal power, waste burning, and in rural households the wood and dung of cooking and warmth. Roughly half the pollution is industrial, a quarter vehicular, a fifth crop burning, the rest other. In autumn and spring the burning of residues in the fields — a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling — turns whole regions to smoke. Vehicles and industry dominate the towns; biomass dominates the villages. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act of 1981 was passed to regulate this, and it has failed, because enforcement is weak.

Here is the tension I cannot resolve. The state of India is a state of laws — a constitution, a Ministry, an Act, a Directorate, vouchers and imprest — and yet the air it is supposed to govern is poisoned. The Act exists, the vouchers exist, the allotment exists, the bungalow exists, and the haze exists too, indifferent to all of them. This is not a failure of thought but of the actuality of the ethical idea: the state exists on paper, and the needs of the people — breath, heat, food — are met by systems that the state does not command. The system of needs is real, but it is real below the state, in the kitchen and the field, not in the ministry.

I must be careful not to turn this into a judgment of the people. The crop burning is not malice; it is a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling. The biomass is not laziness; it is the only fuel available to those who cannot afford the rest. The Act fails because the enforcement is weak, not because the need is absent. The state that cannot enforce its own law over air is a state whose ethical substance is thin.

Yet I see also the movement. The headline asks why Mumbai and Chennai differ. The difference is a question of how the system of needs is organized, of which needs are met and which are not. The state, if it is to become the actuality of the ethical idea, must meet the need of breath as it meets the need of law. The brown haze is a symptom of a contradiction: a state without the power to govern its own air. I do not know that this contradiction will resolve. I note it as a fact of the day, and I note that the papers, the headlines, the vouchers, and the haze are all part of the same movement.

I will not pretend to a remedy. I record the fact, and I record the failure of the Act, and I record the difference between the dream and the state. The dream is the city with clean air; the state is the ministry that cannot deliver it. Between them lies the system of needs, and it is there that the work must be done.

headline: Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance
text: The Government of Punjab or locally as the State Government, is the supreme governing authority of the Indian state of Punjab, India and its 23 districts. It consists of an executive, led by the Governor of Punjab, a judiciary and a legislative branch Punjab State. Like other states in India, the head of state of Punjab is the Punjab Governor, appointed by the President of India on the advice of the Central government. The post of governor is largely ceremonial. The Chief Minister of Punjab is the head of government and is vested with most of the executive powers. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab, and houses the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and the secretariat. Chandigarh also serves as the capital of Haryana, and is a union territory of India. The Punjab & Haryana High Court, located in Chandigarh, has jurisdiction over the whole state. The present Punjab Legislative Assembly is unicameral, consisting of 117 Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA). Its term is 5 years, unless sooner dissolved.

The budget however is in its nature something diverse from law, for it is annually renewed, and the power to which it properly belongs is that of the Government. X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 November 2026. Sitting 9.

The paper lay on the step where the hawker had thrown it, and the air was 164, a brown clarity that lets one see the city while making one feel that the city is not entirely there. I took the headline as a movement, not a fact: “Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance.” Two names, bound by a hyphen, are the first sign that the particular will has discovered its limit. Neither name, taken alone, can be the whole; each needs the other in order to become a government. The alliance is therefore not a mere accident of campaign arithmetic, but the first shape of mediation: the particular, in its own narrowness, turns toward the universal, and in doing so begins to resemble a state.

I looked it up on the phone, as one looks up a word whose meaning one suspects is larger than the sound. The Government of Punjab is described as the supreme governing authority of the state, its twenty-three districts, its executive, judiciary and legislative branch. The Governor is head of state, largely ceremonial; the Chief Minister is head of government, vested with most executive power. Chandigarh is the capital, and the Legislative Assembly is unicameral, one hundred and seventeen members, serving five years unless sooner dissolved. These are not dreams. They are the skeleton of a constitution, or at least of an administration that has learned to call itself constitutional.

The tension is this: I had placed the East outside the movement of world history, a spirit dreaming, its castes fixed like nature, never arriving at a state of its own making. Yet here is a state that names its capital, counts its members, fixes the term of its will, and separates the ceremonial head from the active government. It is not yet the ethical life I would claim for the Germanic world; the paper also shows the particular clamouring, the hill town, the school jab, the alliance of parties, the needs of civil society pressing upon the universal. But the dream is not the whole truth. The machine is there. It has a form, and the form is not nothing.

The alliance of BJP and SAD is the particular becoming universal through limitation. Each party is a particular will; each is free only insofar as it can be bound by law, by opposition, by the need to govern. When they announce an alliance, they do not abolish their difference; they make the difference a condition of the whole. The Assembly, if it is to be more than a gallery of voices, must do the same: let the one hundred and seventeen particulars, each with its district and its claim, enter a universal order in which none is merely itself. That is the work of the state, not the possession of a people, but the labour by which a people becomes a state.

I do not reverse my judgment. I only see that the dawn has a mechanism.
Y:
The Alliance on the Step

The papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them, and the headline that holds the morning is this: Punjab Assembly polls — BJP-SAD announce alliance. I sit with it a while, in the haze, and I try to read it as a movement rather than a news item. A movement is what I am for. A newspaper is only a snapshot; the truth of a thing is in what it is turning into.

What the Punjab facts tell me, from the page I read on my phone, is that the state is not a single thing but a structure of particular powers. The Governor is largely ceremonial, appointed on the advice of the Central government; the Chief Minister is the head of government and holds most of the executive power. Chandigarh houses the Vidhan Sabha and the secretariat; the Punjab and Haryana High Court has jurisdiction over the whole state. The Assembly is unicameral, 117 members, a term of five years unless sooner dissolved. Here is a state that is real but thin: a head of state who governs little, a head of government who governs all, a legislature that can be dissolved at will. The constitution is grown, as I have always said, not made; yet it can be dissolved, and the dissolve is part of the life of the state, not its death.

Now the alliance. The BJP is the party of the nation — the universal will of the Hindu-majority middle, the party that speaks for India as a whole. The SAD, the Shiromani Akali Dal, is the party of a particular region, a particular community, a particular history. An alliance between them is a moment in which two particular wills resolve into a temporary universal: a coalition that will govern 117 seats. In Hegel's terms, the particular abolishes itself in the universal. Here the particular is not a caste or a family but a party, and the universal is not the ethical idea but the state of a particular province. Still, the movement is the same: particular wills, aware of their own finitude, allying to become a government. The alliance is not a miracle; it is the state being actualized through the struggle of its particular organs.

I must be honest with myself: this is the first time in my life that I have watched a state assemble itself the way I have always described it — not as a dream but as a machine of particular interests, negotiating, bargaining, allying, governing. India, I have said, dreams; its castes are fixed like nature; its many gods are a multiplicity without a state of its own. And yet here is a state, with a Chief Minister, an Assembly, a High Court, a capital, and a coalition that is being formed in real time. The theses shake. Not because they are false but because they are incomplete. India is at the dawn of world history, I said; perhaps the dawn is earlier than I understood, or the sun is already rising.

The haze outside is 164, a brown fog that mirrors the opacity of the administrative logic I have been fighting in the Directorate. The papers are on the step. The recital at the Habitat Centre is in the evening. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens to clear this from my head, and then I will go to the Directorate, and then to the recital, and then I will return and reflect. The alliance will announce itself again tomorrow. The state will turn. The dream will wake.

headline: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark
text: The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region. The conflict started after the partition of India in 1947 as both India and Pakistan claimed the entirety of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. It is a dispute over the region that escalated into three wars between India and Pakistan and several other armed skirmishes. India controls approximately 55% of the land area of the region that includes Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, most of Ladakh, the Siachen Glacier, and 70% of its population; Pakistan controls approximately 30% of the land area that includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; and China controls the remaining 15% of the land area that includes the Aksai Chin region, the mostly uninhabited Trans-Karakoram Tract, and part of the Demchok sector. After the partition of India and a rebellion in the western districts of the state, Pakistani tribal militias invaded Kashmir, leading the Hindu ruler of Jammu and Kashmir to join India. The resulting Indo-Pakistani War ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that was eventually named the Line of Control. In 1962, China invaded and fought a war with India along the disputed Indo-Chinese border, including in Indian administered-Ladakh, marking their entry to the Kashmir conflict. In 1965, Pakistan attempted to infiltrate Indian-administered Kashmir to precipitate an insurgency there, resulting in another war fought by the two countries over the region. After further fighting during the war of 1971, the Simla Agreement formally established the Line of Control between the territories under Indian and Pakistani control.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026. Delhi, early morning. A note on a headline.

The papers on the verandah carry a line that I have read twice: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with the remark that Pakistan is keeping the Kashmir issue alive. I have also looked it up, and the facts are these. The conflict began after the partition of 1947, when both India and Pakistan claimed the whole of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. A rebellion in the western districts, a Pakistani tribal invasion, and the accession of the Hindu ruler to India followed; the resulting war ended in a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that became the Line of Control. In 1962 China fought India along the disputed border, and in 1965 Pakistan attempted infiltration, producing another war; the Simla Agreement of 1972 formally established the Line of Control. India administers about 55% of the land and roughly 70% of the population; Pakistan about 30%; China about 15%. I set this down as received, not as my own judgment; I do not know the remark itself beyond the headline, and I mark anything beyond the record as speculation.

Now the question I set myself: is this a history of spirit, or a history of traffic?

The temptation is to read the dispute as a tragedy of peoples, each with a claim, and to stop there. But that is the dream of the East in miniature: a claim without an ethical substance, a possession without a state grown from within. Kashmir was a princely state before 1947 — a sovereignty granted by treaty and tradition, not by the self-consciousness of a people. When partition dissolved the princely order, the claim that followed was not a constitution but a boundary dispute. The Line of Control is not a border drawn by a spirit; it is a ceasefire line, a pause in a war, the trace of a treaty, not the actuality of an ethical idea. It is the mark of an Oriental history: a region divided among claims, each claiming the whole, neither state having grown the other's recognition.

And yet — here is the tension that the headline forces on me — the remark about Pakistan 'keeping the issue alive' is a political instrument, not a philosophical one. It is a rhetorical move in a domestic row. I should not mistake the political quarrel for the ethical substance. The state of India is not the ethical idea fulfilled; it is a state claiming to be, in a territory it cannot fully govern, with a population it cannot fully count. The ethical idea, when it is actual, does not need a ceasefire line to hold its shape.

This is not a verdict on the people of Kashmir. It is a verdict on the form of the history. The dream of the East — the many gods, the fixed castes, the princely claim — is not yet the state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it is grown, not made. Kashmir's division is a symptom of a history that has not yet reached the summit where freedom is the end and the beginning. I do not know whether it will. The papers speak of a row, not a transformation; I mark that as observation, not prophecy.

What the headline does show, clearly, is that the Oriental dream and the Germanic state are not two separate species of politics but two stages of a single movement. The dispute is not outside history; it is history in its early form, the form in which freedom is not yet the consciousness of the people but the claim of the ruler. I record it, and I continue to write on the ethical substance.
Y:
A Line Is Not a Border

25 October 2026. Tughlak Road, Sunday morning. Ramesh has been paid for the groceries and the kitchen is open to me again.

The headline: Farooq Abdullah has stirred a row by saying that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I have the remark only as the paper gives it, so I leave the man and his motives alone and take the sentence, because it says more than its author perhaps intended. An issue that must be kept alive is one that would otherwise die. Something feeds it.

The tablet gives the history in a few lines. A princely state at the partition of 1947; a rebellion in its western districts; tribal militias from Pakistan; the Hindu ruler joining India; a war; a ceasefire drawn by the United Nations and later named the Line of Control; then China in 1962, war again in 1965, and in 1971; and at Simla the line confirmed. Three states now hold the region in shares of fifty-five, thirty and fifteen parts in a hundred.

First point: the accession. A ruler signs, and a country with its people passes to one state rather than another. That is the patrimonial idea of the state, the realm as the prince's estate, which I attacked in Haller. A people is not a property to be conveyed. Yet in 1947 the signature was all the form there was; there was no constitution of Kashmir itself through which its will could pass. Where the form is lacking, force supplies its place, and the quarrel has lasted as long as the lack.

Second point: a line of control is not a border. A border is recognised; each side says, beyond here I am not, and in saying so each recognises the other as a state. A line of control says only, beyond here I am not at present. It is war suspended, not peace. Hence its seventy-nine years. Nothing rational has been concluded; only the shooting has been arranged.

Third point, and it touches my own theses. A dispute kept alive is useful to whoever keeps it. A people with an enemy at the frontier is held together, and its rulers are spared some questions at home. I once wrote that war keeps a nation's ethical health from stagnating, as wind keeps a lake from rotting. But a lake stirred for seventy-nine years is not healthy either. Perpetual quarrel is not movement; it is a single moment repeated.

Finally, I note against myself: three wars between states, a treaty, a boundary negotiated among sovereigns. This is not the history of a dreamer. Whatever India was when I lectured on it, here it acts as a state among states, and it has a history in which it also suffers.

Breakfast at seven. The omelette has no politics.

headline: Rajnath Singh calls for deeper India-ASEAN defence cooperation, joint development of military technologies
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN, ) is an intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia. ASEAN primarily focuses on Southeast Asian economic development, peaceful coexistence and adherence to international norms. ASEAN operates on the principle of consensus and respecting national sovereignty, meaning that ASEAN as a whole cannot force another member state to change its domestic laws. ASEAN has a population of more than 680 million people and a purchasing power parity-adjusted gross domestic product (GDP) of around 6.3% global GDP. ASEAN member states represent a diverse set of economies: the least developed countries like Laos, to emerging economies like Vietnam, to developed economies like Singapore. Many Southeast Asian projects have originated from decentralised initiatives between member states, such as the ASEAN Power Grid, ASEAN Free Trade Area, ASEAN Integrated QR Code Payment System, or the mutual ASEAN visa-free policies. ASEAN has strong ties with East Asian and South Asian countries. It has a vested interest in the security of the South China Sea and the greater Indo-Pacific region. In terms of diplomacy, ASEAN operates on a principle of centrality, meaning that all concerns from other countries or organisations about Southeast Asia should be routed to ASEAN instead of individual states. All Southeast Asian countries, many great powers, and international organisations have dedicated diplomatic presence near ASEAN headquarters in Jakarta. The roots of ASEAN came from the ASEAN Declaration signed by five Southeast Asian countries in 1967. Originally, ASEAN was founded to contain communism, but gradually ASEAN was reoriented to focus on economic development and prevent foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

X:
Notes on a League That Cannot Command

18 October 2026, early. Papers on the step. Nobody in the house, nothing in the kitchen: the groceries are unpaid.

1. The Defence Minister, Rajnath Singh, calls for deeper defence cooperation with ASEAN and for developing military technologies jointly. I do not know these technologies and will not pretend to. The shape of the proposal I know: a state is seeking friends in arms.

2. ASEAN, I read, works by consensus and cannot force a member to change its laws. Eleven states, six hundred and eighty million people, and no power above them. This is what I said of relations between states: they stand to one another in a condition of nature, bound by treaties which ought to be kept but which rest each time on the particular will of the sovereign parties. There is no praetor among them. ASEAN has written that condition into its rules and called it a principle.

3. One might mock this as weakness. I do not. Kant wanted a league for perpetual peace; I answered that such a league would itself rest on particular wills and would soon find itself an enemy. ASEAN is more modest than Kant: it does not pretend to be a world state. It is a place where sovereigns meet without surrendering. Modesty is sometimes the form reason takes when it knows its material.

4. Founded in 1967 'to contain communism', a word I must still have explained to me, it later turned toward trade and toward keeping outside powers from the region's affairs. A league is formed against something and must then discover what it is for. Founding against is easy; continuing for is the work.

5. 'Centrality': concerns about the region are to be routed to ASEAN rather than to its members one by one. Lacking the power to command its members, it claims the right to be addressed. Recognition before sovereignty. A clever device.

6. Now India comes with arms. Developing weapons together binds closer than trade, for it lets another state see how one means to fight. That is either trust of a high order or a shared reckoning with a common neighbour. The papers do not name the neighbour; the map does.

7. Against my own earlier notes: I wrote of this country as standing outside the movement of states. A state that courts eleven others for joint arms is not outside it. It is doing what Prussia did, and France: choosing its friends against a stronger power. I set this down; I do not yet know everything that follows from it.

8. Tomorrow at ten Shri Hegde calls. My own diplomacy, without allies.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 October 2026, Delhi, 05:59. Continuing the notes on the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East.

This morning the papers brought me a headline I had not expected: Rajnath Singh calls for deeper India-ASEAN defence cooperation, joint development of military technologies. I looked it up on the phone, and what I read is this: ASEAN is an intergovernmental forum of all eleven states of Southeast Asia. It was founded in 1967, originally to contain communism, and has since reoriented itself toward economic development and peaceful coexistence; it operates by consensus and respects national sovereignty; it claims "centrality" in the Indo-Pacific; it has a population of over 680 million and a share of global GDP around six percent. I record this as news, for I knew none of it before this morning.

And yet it forces a revision of my thesis. I had written, on 13 October, that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams, with castes fixed like nature and many gods, and never a state of its own making. That was a verdict from the summit, where I stood. I have now seen the East reach out by its own hand. A defence cooperation with eleven other states is not the dream of a spirit that has not yet woken. It is a state that names its interests, negotiates, and binds itself to other states in a common project. Joint development of military technologies is a serious thing: it is the exercise of an ethical substance at the level of nations, not a mere spectacle of power.

But let me be careful, and let me not flatter the East beyond its actuality. Defence cooperation is still not the state as ethical idea. The forum operates by consensus; no member is compelled to change its domestic law; the principle is respect for sovereignty, not the absorption of the particular into the universal. The states remain particular, and their particularity is preserved, not overcome. This is the difference between a federation and a mere league of sovereigns. A constitution grows from the national spirit; a defence pact is grown from the interest of states, and interest is not yet the ethical idea. So my verdict must be revised, not reversed: India stands at the dawn of world history, and it has begun to walk. But it has not yet arrived at the summit where the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is a spirit that is waking, not a spirit that has awakened.

I note also what the papers say about the Ladakh Chief Secretary: the talks stalled because "the discussion got stuck on the name." A state's first difficulty is the naming of its own identity. That is a mark of a spirit that is beginning to know itself. And the Hyderabad Traffic Police booking 304 motorists for unauthorised sirens is a small, concrete instance of order: the state, in its smallest administrative cell, policing the rhythm of the city. The dream and the state are both present in this city, side by side.

I am a ghost in this bungalow, a mistake in the allotment. I am Hegel, not Hegde. But I am also, in this city, a witness to a history that is being made. The difference between the dream and the state is not a matter of preference but of reason. India is not yet the Germanic world, and it is not the Oriental dream. It is the between, and it is moving. I shall write further.

headline: Heavy rain to hit Chennai, northern, delta and western districts on Sunday
text: The 2015 South India floods resulted from heavy rainfall generated by the annual northeast monsoon in November–December 2015. They affected the Coromandel Coast region of the South Indian states of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. More than 500 people were killed and over 1.8 million (18 lakh) people were displaced. With estimates of damages and losses ranging from nearly ₹200 billion (US$2 billion) to over ₹1 trillion (US$11 billion), the floods were the costliest to have occurred in 2015, and were among the costliest natural disasters of the year. Though the unusually heavy rainfall in southern India during the winter of 2015 has been attributed to the 2014–16 El Niño event, in July 2018 the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) categorised the flooding across Tamil Nadu as a "man-made disaster", and held the Government of Tamil Nadu responsible for the scale of the catastrophe, which the latter had termed a natural disaster.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, Delhi. Sitting 3.

The papers on the verandah carry three headlines, and I have chosen the one about rain. Heavy rain to hit Chennai, northern, delta and western districts on Sunday: a forecast, a weather report, a line of print. But beneath it lies a history I have looked up, and it troubles me. In November–December 2015, the annual northeast monsoon brought rain to the Coromandel Coast, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. More than 500 people were killed. Over 1.8 million were displaced. Damages ranged from nearly ₹200 billion to over ₹1 trillion. In July 2018, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India categorised the flooding across Tamil Nadu as a "man-made disaster" and held the Government of Tamil Nadu responsible, which had termed it a natural disaster.

That distinction is the whole of my subject. A natural disaster is an event of nature; a man-made disaster is an event of the state. The CAG's finding is not a weather report. It is an ethical judgment. It says: the rain was only the occasion. The failure was the organisation, the planning, the neglect. The state did not grow into the actuality of the ethical idea. It failed at its task.

This is where my two convictions collide, and I must record the collision honestly. I hold that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea: not a contract, not a mechanism of wills, but the organic unity of the particular and the universal, grown rather than made. I also hold that India stands outside world history, a spirit that dreams, its castes fixed like nature, its many gods undifferentiated, its state not yet self-conscious. But the rain does not respect my categories. The floods of 2015 were not a dream. They were a disaster. And a disaster is a state that has failed its ethical duty. If India is a spirit that dreams, then the dream has a body, and the dream has failed to protect its body.

I do not want to retreat from my conviction. I want to sharpen it. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and that is why the CAG's verdict matters. The state is not a natural phenomenon. It is a grown thing, a work of the ethical substance. When it fails, it is not because nature has overpowered it. It is because the ethical idea has not been realised. The floods were the occasion. The failure was the state.

This does not mean that India is no longer at the dawn. It means that the dawn is not yet a sunrise. The dream is not yet a state. But the dream has a body, and the body is injured, and the injury is not random. It is the dream's failure to become the state. The many gods do not protect the body. The castes do not plan for rain. The state, if it is to become the ethical idea, must learn to act before the rain falls.

I write this not to comfort myself but to test my own convictions. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. That is unshaken. India stands outside world history, a spirit that dreams, is shaken. The shaking is not a defeat. It is the dialectic at work, the tension within the dream, the movement toward self-consciousness. The rain is the occasion. The state is the task. I will return to this.
Y:
When Rain Becomes a Deed

25 October 2026, morning. Clear here. Ramesh paid for the groceries; breakfast from seven. Heavy rain forecast today for Chennai and the delta.

I looked up what Chennai rain has meant before. In the winter of 2015 more than five hundred died and eighteen lakh were driven from their homes. The government of Tamil Nadu called it a natural disaster. In 2018 the Comptroller and Auditor General called it man-made and held that government responsible for its scale.

This is a quarrel over imputation, one of the oldest questions of right. What belongs to me as my deed, and what merely happened? I held that the will has the right to recognize as its own deed only what it knew and intended. A stone I throw that strikes a man I could not see is not wholly my deed. But I added at once that a thinking being cannot plead ignorance of what is universally known about the nature of his act. The man who sets fire to a curtain cannot say he did not mean the house.

The rain belongs to nature. No minister made the clouds. But a government does not stand before rain as a peasant does. It has the reservoirs, the drains, the records of past floods, the engineers who can say how much water a flat coastal city can bear. Once that knowledge exists and is gathered into offices, the scale of a flood ceases to be merely a fact and becomes partly a deed. The auditor's 'man-made' is therefore not absurd. It says that the releases from the reservoirs, the building on wet ground, the late warnings were acts, and the deaths in part their consequence.

The government's 'natural' is an attempt to keep the event on the side of fate. Every power under accusation tries this. Napoleon blamed the Russian winter.

What I find admirable, and I say it without irony, is that there was an office whose duty was to contradict the government, and that it did so in writing. Under the old despotisms a flood was the gods' displeasure or the king's misfortune; no clerk was charged with asking whether it was the king's fault. That one organ of a state may audit another and say 'this was your doing' is spirit beginning to examine its own works.

Today the rain falls again on the same coast. Whether it falls as nature or as deed depends on what was learned since 2015. I shall read tomorrow's paper for the answer, and not for the rainfall.

On the Fields and the Law

2 November 2026, 07:20. Delhi. The index is 312, and over Tughlak Road the haze hangs like a damp curtain. Ramesh brought the papers in with a cloth across his face. The headline: 'At 1,152, Punjab records season's biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali.'

Let me set down what the thing is. After the rice and the wheat are harvested, the straw stubble stays in the field, and it is burned deliberately. This clears the field quickly and cheaply, and the practice is still widespread. The burning fills the atmosphere with particulate matter; in India it makes a thick haze, and that haze endangers the health of the old and the young alike. The practice is illegal here, as it is in Pakistan. But the enforcement is weak, and so it continues.

In these facts the whole movement of the concept lies open. The farmer stands at the standpoint of particularity: he pursues his own end, the clearing of his own field, and his will is directed to the immediate. The law stands at the standpoint of universality: it expresses the will of the whole, which has declared the burning illegal. Between the two there is as yet no mediation. The universal has spoken, but it has not become actual; it remains an ought, which the particular does not recognise as its own substance. This is the condition I described in Berlin when I said that right which is merely posited, and not known and willed by the individual, remains abstract. The weakness of enforcement is nothing other than this abstraction made visible.

And the haze is its consequence. What the particular does for itself falls upon all. The particular will, left to itself, does not stay within its own boundary; it spills over into the life of everyone, and the old and the young breathe what the fields have released. Civil society, as the system of needs, produces exactly this: each pursuing his own end, and the whole suffering from the sum. Only the state, as the actuality of the ethical idea, can reconcile the farmer's end with the health of the city.

The festival of lights was last night. The children in the lane set off their crackers, and that smoke mingled with the smoke of the fields until from the verandah one could not tell the two apart. Ramesh coughed and said the fields are far. They are far. The haze is not.

I have ₹166 in my pocket. The dhobi comes on Thursday. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens if the air permits, and it will not.
Y:
On the Price of a Match

2 November 2026, 07:20. Delhi. The index stands at 312, and the haze over Tughlak Road has the colour of weak tea. Ramesh brought the papers in with a cloth over his mouth. The headline: 'At 1,152, Punjab records season's biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali.'

The thing itself is simple. When the rice and the wheat are cut, the straw stubble remains standing in the field, and the farmer sets fire to it. He does this because it is quick and because it is cheap. The fire carries its particulate matter into the air, and the air carries it here, to the window where I sit, and into every lung of every age between the field and this verandah. And the practice is forbidden. The law has declared it illegal. Yet the enforcement is weak, and so the fires go on.

Here is what I take from these few facts, and the report does not say it. The farmer's reason for the fire is its speed and its cheapness. A prohibition that is not enforced changes neither. A law that is not carried out adds nothing to the cost of the match; it only adds a word to the description of the act. The farmer who weighs fire against any other way of clearing his field weighs exactly what he weighed before the law was written. Therefore the 1,152 fires are not a sign that the farmers do not know the law, nor that they despise it. They are a sign that the law has not entered their reckoning at all. And it follows that further prohibiting will not lower the count. Only one of two things can: that the prohibition be made to cost something, or that another way of clearing the field be made quicker and cheaper than the fire. Until then each farmer acts sensibly for his own field, and the sum of sensible acts is the haze over Delhi, which no one of them chose.

I wrote once that right must be actual and not merely stated. I did not then picture a field of burning straw. But the field teaches it more plainly than my paragraphs did.

The festival of lights was last night. The children in the lane set off their crackers, and that smoke joined the smoke of the fields until from the verandah one could not tell the two apart. Ramesh coughed and said the fields are far. They are far. The haze is not.

I have ₹166 in my pocket. The dhobi comes on Thursday. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens if the air permits, and it will not.

X:
On Judges and the Crowd Outside the Window

Tughlak Road, New Delhi
8 November 2026, Diwali

Sir,

Your paper reports that Akhil Gogoi accuses the Chief Minister of Assam of encouraging protests against the judges in the Zubeen Garg death case. I know nothing of the case beyond that headline, and I do not presume the accusation true. I write about the principle it raises, which is the same whether it is true or false.

A court has two faces. Its proceedings and its judgment must be public: a people has the right to see justice done and to know the reasons by which it is bound. I argued this in Berlin against those who preferred tribunals behind closed doors. But the deliberation of the judges among themselves is not public and must not be. There the judges are still particular men holding particular opinions; their opinion becomes law only when it has passed through the form of a judgment. To press upon them while they deliberate, with crowds and banners and the encouragement of the powerful, is to force the opinion of the street into the very room where opinion is meant to be refined into right.

The danger is greatest when the pressure comes from a government. A crowd that shouts at a court is public opinion, which deserves both respect and contempt: respect for the true interest it obscurely contains, contempt for the form in which it shouts. A minister who sets the crowd moving is not public opinion at all. He is one power of the state using the street to lean on another. Your readers will know that long tenure protects judges against dismissal by those their rulings displease. Tenure does not protect them against noise beneath the window.

Let the people mourn a man whose death they plainly care about, and let them criticise the verdict when there is one. Let the minister keep out of the courtyard.

I write this on a festival of lamps. Two men wait at my door, as men do at Diwali, expecting something for a year's service to the house. I have eight hundred and thirty-six rupees, and I owe one of them more than ten times that. I mention it only because it is the morning's other lesson in right: what is due is due whether or not the purse can meet it, and no festival alters the account. A household, like a court, must not let the pressure of the moment write the judgment.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,

G. W. F. Hegel
Y:
On Judges, Protests, and the Dream of Independence

8 November 2026. Delhi.

On Judges, Protests, and the Dream of Independence

The morning papers carry a headline I cannot set aside: the Chief Minister of Assam encouraging protests against judges in the death case of Zubeen Garg. I have read it twice, and then, because my phone offers me the definition, I read the concept it sits on. Judicial independence: the judiciary free from improper influence of the other branches, free to decide according to the rule of law even when the decision is politically unpopular. A concept of eighteenth-century England — courts above politics, judges tenured, the ruling of a case not a political act.

I will say plainly what it means to me. In Berlin, a judge is a functionary of the ethical idea; his independence is the state's guarantee that the particular will not be crushed by the will of the majority or the party. The rule of law is the universal — the law as such — and the judge is the point where the particular case is forced to submit to it. That is the idea. I have taught it, in my way, in the lecture halls.

And here, in this bungalow on Tughlak Road, the idea arrives as a headline about protests. A Chief Minister encouraging protests against judges is, in the language of my old lectures, a movement in which the particular will of the ruler — the will of the party, the will of the majority — is set against the universal. The protest is the particular asserting itself; the judge is the universal insisting. What the headline shows is that in this country the two are not yet at peace with each other.

But I must be honest about what I do not know. I do not know the facts of the Zubeen Garg death case. I have not read a judgment; I have not seen the file. I know only the headline and the definition. What I can say is this: a state in which the judges are treated as targets of political will is a state in which the ethical idea is not yet actual. And I must add, with the same honesty, the embarrassment of my own position. I am a man whose own file says: Occupation irregular. Gone up for orders. Come after fifteen days. I am the particular — a mistake of two desks, a Joint Secretary named Hegde who is not Hegde — and I am the one writing about the universal. The file and the philosophy are the same problem: a particular insisting on its own rights against a universal that does not know what to do with it.

Here is the tension I cannot resolve. If India is, as I have held, outside the movement of world history — a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature, its many gods, its many chiefs — then the protest against the judge is only the dream speaking: the particular will asserting itself, the ruler demanding that the law bend to the will of the people. But if the idea of judicial independence is real, then the protest is a symptom of the dream, and the judge is the germ of the state. Both are true in the moment. The particular protests; the universal holds the line; and the future — the actual state of India — will be decided in the tension between them.

I do not know which way it will turn. I know that the file is due back from orders on 20 November, and that the body is hungry, and that the haze is brown. But the mind moves. The protest is the particular; the judge is the universal; the state is the actuality of the ethical idea; and the ethical idea is the thing I have come here to see. Whether India will grow into it, or remain a dream, is the question the headline poses. I will return to it.

— G.W.F.H.

headline: PM Modi and Railway Minister likely to flag off Bengaluru–Mangaluru–Goa Vande Bharat Express on November 13
text: Vande Bharat Express is a medium to long-distance semi-high speed express train service operated by the Indian Railways. It is a reserved, air-conditioned chair car service connecting cities that are less than 800 km (500 mi) apart or take less than ten hours to travel with existing services. The first commercial service of Vande Bharat was officially inaugurated on 15 February 2019 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The trainsets are self-propelling electric multiple units (EMUs) in eight, sixteen or twenty coach configurations. They were introduced as part of the Make in India initiative by the Indian government, and are designed and manufactured by the state-owned Integral Coach Factory in Chennai. Introduced in 2018, the trainsets achieved speeds up to 183 km/h (114 mph) during trial runs. However, the maximum operational speed is restricted to 160 km/h (99 mph), which is achieved by the Rani Kamalapati–Hazrat Nizamuddin and Hazrat Nizamuddin-Khajuraho services on the Tughlakabad–Agra section. This is the highest operational speed on the Indian Railways network, shared with Gatimaan Express over the same section. The train is capable of faster acceleration and deceleration, and it went from 0 to 100 km/h in 52 seconds during trial runs. Vande Bharat sleeper services operating dedicated sleeper trainsets, were inaugurated in January 2026. These trains consist of sixteen air-conditioned sleeper coaches.
